title: DOAH 26-0046 Recommended Order: HOLLY KELLER vs. HAIR MECHANIX
text:
STATE OF FLORIDA
DIVISION OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
HOLLY KELLER,
Petitioner,
vs. Case No. 26-0046
HAIR MECHANIX,
Respondent.
/
RECOMMENDED ORDER
The final hearing in this matter was conducted before Lynne A. Quimby-
Pennock, Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) of the Division of Administrative
Hearings (DOAH), pursuant to sections 120.569 and 120.57(1), Florida
Statutes (2025), on March 18, 2026, via Zoom video conference, from
Tallahassee, Florida.
APPEARANCES
For Petitioner: Holly Raye Keller, pro se
800 Exchange State Road
Attica, New York 14011
For Respondent: Mark Atherholt, Esquire
M. Sean Moyles, Esquire
Langston, Hess, Augustine,
Sojourner & Moyles, P.A.
600 Druid Road East
Clearwater, Florida 33756
STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES
Whether Respondent, Hair Mechanix (Mechanix), discriminated against
Petitioner, Holly Keller, on the basis of her sex, or age, and retaliated against

her by terminating her employment, in violation of the Florida Civil Rights
Act.
PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
On June 17, 2025, Petitioner filed an Employment Complaint of
Discrimination (Complaint) with the Florida Commission on Human
Relations (FCHR), alleging Mechanix discriminated against her based on her
age or sex, and retaliated against her, in violation of chapter 760, Florida
Statutes, the Florida Civil Rights Act (FCRA).
On December 12, 2025, FCHR issued a determination that no reasonable
cause existed to believe that Respondent had committed an unlawful
employment practice. On December 26, 2025, Petitioner filed a Petition for
Relief (Petition) with FCHR alleging Respondent engaged in discriminatory
employment practices.
On January 5, 2026, FCHR referred the Petition to DOAH, where it was
assigned to the undersigned. After the failure of either party to timely
respond to the Initial Order, the undersigned issued a Notice setting the final
hearing for February 16, 2026, by Zoom conference.1 A duly noticed Status
Conference was held on February 3, 2026. Thereafter the parties jointly
requested a referral to mediation. This matter was set for an Alternative
Dispute Resolution (ADR) conference before a different assigned ALJ. The
report from the ADR settlement conference provided that no resolution was
reached and the matter “should proceed to final hearing.”
The matter was rescheduled to March 18, 2026, and completed on that
day. At the hearing, Petitioner testified on her own behalf and presented the
1 In late January 2026, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis announced that all state offices
would be closed on Monday, February 16, 2026, in observance of President’s Day.
2

testimony of Jasmina Kosarac (Mina).2 Petitioner’s Exhibits 5 through 73
were admitted into evidence. Respondent presented the testimony of
Dennis Hostacky, Luis Fonseca, and Daniel Xikis. Respondent’s Exhibits 64
and 8 were received into evidence.
Prior to testimony being heard, Respondent’s counsel offered a motion
about the scope of the hearing. The undersigned denied the motion and the
hearing proceeded to conclusion.
A court reporter recorded the final hearing. Neither party ordered a
transcript. At the end of the hearing, the parties were advised of the ten-day
timeframe following the hearing to file post-hearing submittals. Neither
party requested additional time in which to file their submittals. The parties
were advised that their proposed recommended orders (PROs) were due by
the close of business on Monday, March 30, 2026, as the tenth day after the
hearing fell on a weekend.
Both parties timely filed PROs, which were duly considered in preparing
this Recommended Order. To the extent there were facts or information that
were not presented under oath and subjected to cross-examination during the
hearing, those matters have been excluded from consideration.
In making the findings below, the undersigned only considered hearsay
evidence that supplemented or explained other evidence or would be
2 Mina was subpoenaed by Petitioner. However, Mina was also listed as a witness for
Respondent. In order to allow Mina to return to her daily activities, both parties were
allowed to elicit testimony from her when she was first called to testify.
3 Petitioner’s Exhibits 5 and 6 were admitted into evidence without objection. Exhibit 7 was
admitted over objection. Petitioner’s Exhibit 8 was not admitted into evidence.
4 Respondent’s Exhibit 6 was admitted over objection.
3

admissible over objection in civil actions. § 120.57(1)(c), Fla. Stat. Unless
stated otherwise, all statutory references shall be to that version of the
Florida Statutes in effect at the time of the allegations.
FINDINGS OF FACT
Based on the oral and documentary evidence adduced at the final hearing
and reasonable inferences drawn from the totality of all the evidence, the
following Findings of Fact are made:
Witnesses
1. Petitioner is a female Florida licensed barber. At some time in the past
she also held a cosmetology license.
2. Petitioner’s FCHR complaint listed age, sex, and retaliation as the basis
for her employment discrimination. However, Petitioner’s Petition focused on
the retaliation claim in that she “engaged in a protected activity by objecting
to and refusing to participate in services she reasonably believed were
outside the legal scope of her professional license under Florida law.”
3. Hair Mechanix is a locally owned Barber shop (Shop) in Pinellas
County, Florida. The Shop is one of two shops owned by Mr. Fonseca.
However, the number of employees of the Shop, where the alleged
discrimination occurred, was never disclosed. There is a corporate structure,
but the extent of it was not disclosed.
4. Mr. Hostacky is a former manager of the Shop and served in that
capacity during the time of the alleged incident.
5. Mina, who is 54 years old, is a licensed cosmetologist who worked in the
Shop at the same time as Petitioner.
6. Mr. Xikis was a client in the Shop on May 30, 2025. He is a restaurant
manager who has experience working with employees and establishing a
good working environment.
7. Melissa Perella is a management employee of the Shop. Ms. Perella did
not testify, but her name was mentioned by other witnesses.
4

Case Development
8. Petitioner began working at Mechanix in March 2025, as a Florida
licensed barber, with over 30 years of experience.
9. Petitioner signed a contract as an independent contractor (a 1099
contractor) who rented a chair in the Shop. She was required to have all her
own tools necessary to work. The Shop provided shampoo, conditioner, and
several other products for the Shop employees to use. Petitioner provided her
desired work days and her preference of working full days, mornings,
afternoons, or a combination. The Shop’s website presence reflected
Petitioner’s schedule.
10. Petitioner observed cosmetologists performing straight razor shaves.
She had concerns regarding cosmetologists performing straight razor shaves
which she believed required barber training. Petitioner first expressed this
concern to Mr. Fonseca and then to Ms. Perella.
11. At some point a client was booked through the online booking website
for Petitioner to perform a waxing service. Petitioner advised Mr. Hostacky
that she did not want to perform waxing services, because of her licensure
constraints. However, Petitioner did perform waxing services on that one
occasion because she was directed to do so by Mr. Hostacky.
12. Petitioner’s second concern involved these waxing services being
attributed to barbers. Petitioner requested that waxing services be removed
from her service profile on the company’s website because of her licensing
concerns.
Issue of the Case
13. On May 30, 2025, Petitioner was present in the Shop. At the same
time, a co-worker, Mina, was also in the Shop.
14. Mr. Xikis received a voucher to go to the Shop. He booked his services
for the first available person for a haircut, “the whole nine yards.” Mr. Xikis
wanted to make a good impression at a new restaurant opening he was
required to attend in Georgia.
5

15. Mina was the available stylist to have Mr. Xikis as a client. As Mina
was washing Mr. Xikis’s hair, he asked for additional services to include nose,
ear, and eyebrow waxing. Mina was upfront with Mr. Xikis by stating that
she (Mina) was not comfortable in performing the waxing services. Mina told
Mr. Xikis that she (Mina) would ask her co-worker (Petitioner) to do the
waxing services.
16. Mina asked Petitioner to perform the waxing services. Mina assured
Petitioner that she would get credit for doing the service, but Petitioner
declined to do so. Their dialogue went on for some time.
17. Mina felt frustrated and scared during the back and forth exchange
with Petitioner over her refusal to perform the waxing services. Mina also
thought Petitioner was rude in front of Mr. Xikis, and Mina apologized to
Mr. Xikis several times.
18. Mr. Xikis credibly testified that Petitioner was just not willing to help
Mina. Further, Mr. Xikis testified Petitioner was being rude and disrespectful
to Mina. Mr. Xikis felt embarrassed for the Shop. Mina was very apologetic
through the entirety of the altercation with Petitioner.
19. Mr. Xikis’s experiences in the food management industry provided
that these types of altercations between co-workers happen all the time.
However, when guests are in your establishment, right in front of you, there
are just some things you do not do, including being unprofessional. You just
do not want employees representing your brand in a negative way.
20. Mr. Xikis complemented Mina in saying she acted as a professional
should under the circumstances and she was very apologetic throughout it.
Further, Mr. Xikis never heard Petitioner’s claim of licensing concerns as her
basis for refusing to perform the waxing services.
21. Mr. Xikis further credibly testified that he had “great service” and has
gone back to the Shop because of their attention to detail.
22. Mr. Xikis left the Shop and Mina contacted management about the
altercation. She described the altercation and expressed that Petitioner was
6

rude in front of a client. Mina was very frustrated that Petitioner would not
help by performing the waxing services.
23. After the discussion with Mina, Mr. Fonseca then contacted
Mr. Hostacky and asked him to contact the client to find out if the client had
witnessed or heard the altercation.
24. Later that day, Mr. Hostacky contacted Mr. Xikis about the service he
received at the Shop. Mr. Xikis confirmed he was at the Shop, and added he
had witnessed the altercation between Mina and Petitioner. Mr. Xikis
provided that Mina asked Petitioner to perform the waxing services, and
Petitioner declined. Initially the tone of the conversation started out in a
passive aggressive manner. However, Petitioner’s tone became more and
more aggressive as the altercation between the two continued.
25. Mr. Xikis provided that there was definitely tension between
Petitioner and Mina, and that Petitioner was being unprofessional in her
response to the requested assistance. Mr. Xikis expressed that he could see
there were two sides to the altercation, but when a customer is in the
building, you have to put the customer first; you are representing a company
that is trying to build the business up, not tear it down.
26. Mr. Xikis testified he was uncomfortable and embarrassed for Mina as
the altercation continued.
Petitioner’s Employment Termination
27. Mr. Fonseca spoke with Mr. Hostacky who provided that Mr. Xikis
corroborated Mina’s account of the altercation in the Shop. The decision was
made to terminate Petitioner’s employment based on the altercation in front
of a client that got very uncomfortable and was unprofessional. The decision
was made for what was best for the Shop.
28. The following morning, May 31, 2025, Petitioner’s employment was
terminated.
29. For clarity, Petitioner testified that she was not alleging age or gender
discrimination in her Petition, as was set forth in her Complaint.
7

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
30. DOAH has jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter of this
cause under sections 120.569, 120.57(1), and 760.11(7). See Fla. Admin. Code
R. 60Y-4.016.
31. The FCRA protects individuals from discrimination in the workplace.
Section 760.10 states:
(1) It is an unlawful employment practice for an
employer:
(a) To discharge ... or otherwise to discriminate
against any individual with respect to
compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of
employment, because of such individual’s ... sex, ...
age.
32. FCRA also protects employees from certain retaliatory acts. FCRA’s
anti-retaliation provision is found in section 760.10(7) and states, in
pertinent part:
It is an unlawful employment practice for an
employer … to discriminate against any person
because that person has opposed any practice which
is an unlawful employment practice under this
section, or because that person has made a charge,
testified, assisted, or participated in any manner in
an investigation, proceeding, or hearing under this
section.
33. Section 760.02(7) provides the following definition:
“Employer” means any person employing 15 or more
employees for each working day in each of 20 or more
calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar
year, and any agent of such a person.
34. Section 760.11(7) permits a party for whom FCHR determines that
there is no reasonable cause to believe that a violation of FCRA has occurred
to request an administrative hearing before DOAH. Following an
8

administrative hearing, if the ALJ finds that a discriminatory act has
occurred, the ALJ “shall issue an appropriate recommended order to the
commission prohibiting the practice and recommending affirmative relief
from the effects of the practice, including back pay.” § 760.11(7), Fla. Stat.
35. The burden of proof in an administrative proceeding, absent a
statutory directive to the contrary, is on the party asserting the affirmative of
the issue. Dep’t of Transp. v. J.W.C. Co., 396 So. 2d 778 (Fla. 1st DCA 1981);
see also Dep’t of Banking & Fin., Div. of Sec. & Investor Prot. v. Osborne
O‘Stern & Co., 670 So. 2d 932, 935 (Fla. 1996) (“The general rule is that a
party asserting the affirmative of an issue has the burden of presenting
evidence as to that issue.”). Thus, Petitioner bears the burden of proving her
allegations of discrimination. The preponderance of the evidence standard is
applicable to this matter. See § 120.57(1)(j), Fla. Stat. See also Fla. Dep’t of
Transp. v. J.W.C. Co., 396 So. 2d 778 (Fla. 1st DCA 1981).
36. FCRA is patterned after Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as
amended. Accordingly, Florida courts hold that federal decisions construing
Title VII, including claims of retaliation, are applicable when considering
claims under FCRA. Harper v. Blockbuster Ent. Corp., 139 F.3d 1385, 1387
(11th Cir. 1998); Valenzuela v. GlobeGround N. Am., LLC, 18 So. 3d 17, 21
(Fla. 3d DCA 2009); Reis v. Universal City Dev. Partners, Ltd., 442 F. Supp.
2d 1238, 1252 (M.D. Fla. 2006); and Eliassaint v. RTG Furniture Corp., 551
F. Supp. 3d 1293, 1302 (M.D. Fla. 2021).
37. Discrimination may be proven by direct, statistical, or circumstantial
evidence. Valenzuela, 18 So. 3d at 22. Direct evidence is evidence that, “if
believed, proves [the] existence of [a] fact in issue without inference or
presumption.” Burrell v. Bd. of Trs. of Ga. Mil. Coll., 125 F.3d 1390, 1393
(11th Cir. 1997). Direct evidence consists of “only the most blatant remarks,
whose intent could be nothing other than to discriminate” on the basis of an
impermissible factor. Carter v. City of Miami, 870 F.2d 578, 582 (11th Cir.
1989).
9

38. There is no direct evidence regarding the size of the Shop or the
number of employees who worked for the Shop. There is no direct evidence
that any unlawful discrimination in the instant case. The record in this
matter does not contain direct evidence of sex or age discrimination or
retaliation on the part of Respondent. Similarly, the record in this proceeding
contains no statistical evidence of discrimination by the Shop.
39. In the absence of direct or statistical evidence of discriminatory intent,
Petitioner must rely on circumstantial evidence to prove a claim of
discrimination. For discrimination causes of action as to Petitioner’s sex, or
age involving circumstantial evidence, Florida courts follow the three-part,
burden-shifting framework set forth in McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green,
411 U.S. 792 (1973), and its progeny. Valenzuela, 18 So. 3d at 21-22; and
St. Louis v. Fla. Int’l Univ., 60 So. 3d 455, 458 (Fla. 3d DCA 2011).
40. The complainant has the initial burden of establishing by a
preponderance of the evidence a prima facie case of unlawful discrimination.
Failure to establish a prima facie case ends the inquiry. If, however, the
complainant succeeds in making a prima facie case, then the burden shifts to
the accused employer to articulate a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for
its complained-of conduct. If the employer carries this burden, then the
complainant must establish that the proffered reason was not the true reason
but merely a pretext for discrimination. Id., St. Mary’s Honor Center v. Hicks,
509 U.S. 502, 506-07 (1993); Valenzuela, 18 So. 3d 17, 25 (Fla. 3rd DCA 2009)
(explaining that in order to establish that the proffered reason was
pretextual, the complainant must present evidence sufficient to cause a
finder-of-fact to infer that the employer was probably motivated by a
discriminatory reason or that the proffered reason lacked credibility).
41. Petitioner did not make a prima facie case of discrimination. Even if
she had, Respondent articulated a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason for
terminating her employment. See Lin v. Demings, 219 So. 3d 124, 125 (Fla.
5th DCA 2017); Valenzuela, 18 So. 3d 17 at 22. The proffered reason for the
10

employer’s decision should be clear, reasonably specific, and worthy of
credence. Dep’t of Corr. v. Chandler, 582 So. 2d 1183, 1186 (Fla. 1st DCA
1991).
42. Petitioner provided no evidence that Mechanix’s reasons for her
employment termination were “weak, implausible, inconsistent, incoherent,
or contradicted by the facts.” Chapman v. A.I. Transp., 229 F.3d 1012, 1030
(11th Cir. 2000). Respondent has not met her burden of establishing
discrimination or retaliation.
RECOMMENDATION
Based on the foregoing Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, it is
RECOMMENDED that the Florida Commission on Human Relations issue a
final order dismissing Holly Keller’s Petition for Relief.
DONE AND ENTERED this 6th day of April, 2026, in Tallahassee, Leon
County, Florida.

title: DOAH 26-0048 Recommended Order: TYKEAL GALERY vs. JAMES BRODICK
text:
STATE OF FLORIDA
DIVISION OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
TYKEAL GALERY,
Petitioner,
vs. Case No. 26-0048
REALTY PROS ASSURED, LLC; AND
JAMES BRODICK,
Respondents.
/
RECOMMENDED ORDER
Pursuant to notice, a final hearing was conducted on March 13, 2026, via
Zoom before Garnett W. Chisenhall, a duly designated Administrative Law
Judge of the Division of Administrative Hearings (“DOAH”).
APPEARANCES
For Petitioner: Tykeal Galery, pro se
399 Smithfield Street
Dillonvale, Ohio 43917
For Respondent: Sven L. Smith, Esquire
Mahshie & Decosta, P.A.
900 West Granada Boulevard, Suite 3
Ormond Beach, Florida 32174
STATEMENT OF THE ISSUE
Whether the Florida Fair Housing Act (“the Act”) was violated on May 29,
2025, during a telephone conversation between Petitioner and Respondent
James Brodick.

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
On September 28, 2025, Petitioner (“Tykeal Galery”) filed a Housing
Discrimination Complaint with the Florida Commission on Human Relations
(“the Commission”) setting forth the following allegations:
Complainant Tykeal Galery is in the process of
selling his home. As such, [Mr. Galery] belongs to a
class of persons whom [the Act] protects from
unlawful discrimination by virtue of Race.
[Mr. Galery] owns a home located at 600 Holmes
Avenue Daytona Beach, FL 32115. Respondent
James Brodick was identified by [Mr. Galery] as the
realtor that works for Respondent Realty Pros
Assured, LLC.
[Mr. Galery] alleged that on May 13, 2025,
Respondent James Brodick sent a text message that
“some people are scared of that neighborhood” and
he would not live at the subject property with his
children due to poorly rated schools in the area.
[Mr. Galery] alleged that on May 29, 2025, he had a
showing of the subject property with a potential
buyer, who is Black. [Mr. Galery] also alleged that
on May 29, 2025, Respondent James Brodick sent a
text message to ask “what color are they?” in
reference to the potential buyer. Respondent James
Brodick also texted that “that’s a good place for them
to be: after [Mr. Galery] confirmed that the person
that viewed the subject property was Black. [Mr.
Galery] alleged that on June 6, 2025, he sent a letter
to request the termination of the Real Estate
Agreement with Respondent James Brodick and
Respondent Realty Pros Assured, LLC. [Mr. Galery]
believes that Respondent James Brodick was
steering only Black potential buyers towards
viewing his home. As such, [Mr. Galery] believes
that the Respondents have subjected him to
discriminatory terms, conditions, privileges, or
services, discrimination in
terms/conditions/privileges relating to sale, and
steering due to race.
2

On December 23, 2025, the Commission issued a Notice concluding that
"reasonable cause does not exist to believe that a discriminatory housing
practice has occurred.” Mr. Galery responded by filing a Petition for Relief,
and the Commission referred this matter to DOAH on January 5, 2026.
The undersigned issued a Notice on January 20, 2026, scheduling the
final hearing for March 13, 2026.
On March 4, 2026, Mr. Galery filed a “Motion for Pre-Hearing
Stipulations” asserting “[t]his case concerns the statements made during the
May 29, 2025 telephone call between [Mr. Galery] and Respondent Brodick.”
The undersigned denied the Motion for Pre-Hearing Stipulations via an
Order issued on March 11, 2026. In doing so, the undersigned noted that “at
the outset of the final hearing, the undersigned will question the parties
about narrowing the scope of the evidentiary presentations to an alleged
phone call that occurred on May 29, 2025.”
The final hearing was convened as scheduled. At the outset, the
undersigned announced that the parties’ dispute was limited to a May 29,
2025, phone call between Mr. Galery and Mr. Brodick. Accordingly, the
undersigned elected to only accept Respondent’s Exhibit 2 into evidence.
Mr. Galery testified on his own behalf, and Respondents presented testimony
from Mr. Brodick.
The one-volume final hearing Transcript was filed on April 3, 2026.
Both parties filed timely Proposed Recommended Orders that were
considered in the preparation of this Recommended Order.
Unless stated otherwise, all references shall be to the 2024 version of the
Florida Statutes. See McClosky v. Dep’t of Fin. Serv., 115 So. 3d 441 (Fla. 5th
3

DCA 2013) (standing for the proposition that a proceeding is governed by the
law in effect at the time of the commission of the acts alleged to constitute a
violation of law).
FINDINGS OF FACT
Based on the oral and documentary evidence adduced at the final hearing,
the entire record of this proceeding, and matters subject to official
recognition, the following Findings of Fact are made:
1. Realty Pros Assured, LLC (“Realty Pros”) is a Florida real estate
brokerage, and Mr. Brodick is a licensed Florida sales associate affiliated
with Realty Pros.
2. Mr. Galery identifies as a Native American and an African American.
3. In April of 2025, Mr. Galery retained Realty Pros to assist with the sale
of his home in Daytona Beach, Florida. The sales price began at $225,000.
On April 21, 2025, the price was lowered to $216,900, and it was lowered
again on May 14, 2025, to $214,000.
4. On May 29, 2025, two different prospective buyers toured Mr. Galery’s
home. After the tours had been completed, Mr. Galery and Mr. Brodick had a
telephone conversation. According to Mr. Galery, Mr. Brodick inquired about
the prospective buyers’ race, and Mr. Galery interpreted that question to be
an indication that Mr. Brodick believed the home was inappropriate for
Caucasians. Mr. Brodick claims he was merely attempting to ascertain the
identity of an agent who had accompanied one of the buyers.
5. While there is no evidence indicating that Mr. Galery’s version of the
May 29, 2025, telephone conversation is not truthful, the undersigned is
unable to find that Mr. Galery’s version is more credible that Mr. Brodick’s.
6. Mr. Galery ultimately sold his home in October of 2025 for $176,500.
7. During the final hearing, Mr. Galery was unable to identify how he was
harmed by any actions or omissions by Mr. Brodick. For example, Mr. Galery
4

did not testify that he was forced to accept a lower price for his home due to
any actions or omissions by Mr. Brodick.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
8. DOAH has jurisdiction over the parties to and the subject matter of this
proceeding. § 120.57(1), Fla. Stat.
9. The Act, sections 760.20 through 760.37, Florida Statutes, prohibits
discrimination in matters, pertaining to a dwelling, on the basis of a person’s
race. The Act is patterned after Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, as
amended by the Fair Housing Act of 1988, and discrimination covered under
the Act is the same discrimination prohibited under the Federal Fair Housing
Act. Savannah Club Worship Serv., Inc. v. Savannah Club Homeowners’
Ass’n, Inc., 456 F. Supp. 2d 1223, 1224 n.1 (S.D. Fla. 2005). When “a Florida
Statute is modeled after a federal law on the same subject, the Florida
statute will take on the same constructions as placed on its federal prototype,
insofar as such interpretation is harmonious with the spirit and policy of the
Florida legislation.” Brand v. Fla. Power Corp., 633 So. 2d 504, 509 (Fla. 1st
DCA 1994).
10. In the instant case, Mr. Galery has the burden of establishing, by a
preponderance of the evidence, that a violation of the Act occurred.
§ 760.34(5), Fla. Stat.; Fla. Dep’t of Transp. v. J.W.C. Co., 396 So. 2d 778
(Fla. 1st DCA 1981).
11. Before assessing the merits of Mr. Galery’s discrimination claim, the
undersigned must assess whether Mr. Galery has standing. Even though
Respondents did not argue that Mr. Galery lacks standing, the undersigned
still has an obligation to make that determination. See generally Fla. Ass’n of
Med. Equip. Dealers v. Apfel, 194 F.3d 1227, 1230 (11th Cir. 1999)(stating
that “every court has an independent duty to review standing as a basis for
jurisdiction at any time, for every case it adjudicates.”); AT&T Mobility, LLC
v. Nat’l Ass’n of Stock Car Auto Racing, Inc., 494 F.3d 1356, 1360 (11th Cir.
5

2007)(stating that “we are obliged to consider standing sua sponte even if the
parties have not raised the issue because an appellate court must satisfy
itself not only of its own jurisdiction, but also of that of the lower courts in a
cause under review.”).
12. The plain language of the Act appears to require that a petitioner
must have suffered, or is about to suffer, an injury prior to filing a housing
discrimination claim. § 760.34(1), Fla. Stat. (providing that “[a]ny person who
claims to have been injured by a discriminatory housing practice or who
believes that he or she will be injured by a discriminatory housing practice
that is about to occur may file a complaint with the [C]ommission.”)(emphasis
added). See also Herbozo and Liesenfeld v. Fernandez, 2026 WL 706678, at *3
(M.D. Fla. 2026)(noting that “[a]lthough standing under the Fair Housing Act
is notoriously broad, it almost certainly does not stretch so far as to allow
plaintiffs to assert claims for alleged discrimination in apartment complexes
that they do not live in or seek to live in.”); Wheatley Heights Neighborhood
Coal. v. Jenna Resales Co., 429 F. Supp. 486, 489 (E.D. N.Y. 1977)(concluding
the plaintiffs had standing to maintain a Fair Housing Act claim based on
allegations that plaintiffs suffered the following injuries: “they do not reside
in a racially stable community, they find it more difficult to sell their homes
because defendants steer prospective white purchasers away from Wheatley
Heights, and their property values will decline should these practices
continue.”).
13. In his Housing Discrimination Complaint and Petition for Relief,
Mr. Galery does not allege that he was injured, in any way, by any actions or
omissions by Mr. Brodick. During the final hearing, Mr. Galery was unable to
answer whether any of Mr. Brodick’s actions or omissions impaired his ability
to sell his home for his desired price. As a result, the undersigned concludes
that Mr. Galery lacks standing because there is no evidence that he has been
injured by a discriminatory housing practice.
6

14. In addition, even if Mr. Galery had set forth allegations indicating that
he had been injured by a discriminatory housing practice, he failed to
demonstrate, by a preponderance of the evidence, that Respondents violated
the Act.
15. Mr. Galery’s allegations amount to a claim of racial steering. The U.S.
Supreme Court has defined “racial steering” as “directing prospective home
buyers interested in equivalent properties to different areas according to
their race.” Gladstone Realtors v. Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91, (1979).
16. Relevant portions of section 760.23(2), (3), and (4) provide that:
(2) It is unlawful to discriminate against any person
in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or
rental of a dwelling, or in the provision of services or
facilities in connection therewith, because of race,
color, national origin, sex, handicap, familial status
or religion.
(3) It is unlawful to make, print, or publish, or cause
to be made, printed, or published, any notice,
statement, or advertisement with respect to the sale
or rental of a dwelling that indicates any preference,
limitation, or discrimination based on race, color,
national origin, sex, disability, familial status, or
religion or an intention to make any such preference,
limitation, or discrimination.
(4) It is unlawful to represent to any person because
of race, color, national origin, sex, disability, familial
status, or religion that any dwelling is not available
for inspection, sale, or rental when such dwelling is
in fact so available.
17. Section 760.25(2)(a) provides that
[i]t is unlawful for any person or entity whose
business includes engaging in residential real estate
transactions to discriminate against any person in
making available such a transaction, or in the terms
or conditions of such a transaction, because of race,
color, national origin, sex, disability, familial status,
or religion.
7

18. Section 760.25(2)(b) defines “residential real estate transaction” to
include “[t]he selling, brokering, or appraising of residential real property.”
19. Because the undersigned did not find that Mr. Galery’s description of
the May 29, 2025, telephone conversation was more credible than
Mr. Brodick’s, Mr. Galery did not prove that Respondents violated the Act.
RECOMMENDATION
Based on the foregoing Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, it is
RECOMMENDED that the Florida Commission on Human Relations issue a
final order dismissing Tykeal Galery’s Housing Discrimination Complaint

County, Florida.

title: DOAH 26-0051 Recommended Order: RONNIE ROBERTS vs. MIAMI INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT
text:
STATE OF FLORIDA
DIVISION OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
RONNIE ROBERTS,
Petitioner,
vs. Case No. 26-0051
MIAMI INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT,
Respondent.
/
RECOMMENDED ORDER
Pursuant to notice, a final hearing in this case was conducted before
Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”) Mary Li Creasy of the Division of
Administrative Hearings (“DOAH”) by Zoom conference on April 8, 2026.
APPEARANCES
For Petitioner: Ronnie L. Roberts, pro se
1287 Hopewell Road
Morganton, North Carolina 28655
For Respondent: Narinah P. Jean-Baptiste, Esquire
Miami-Dade County Attorney’s Office
111 Northwest 1st Street, Suite 2810
Miami, Florida 33134
STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES
Whether Petitioner was unlawfully discriminated against by denial of
assistive services (wheelchair access and disability seating) at the Miami
airport in violation of the Florida Civil Rights Act (“FCRA”); and, if so, what
is the appropriate remedy.

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
On June 10, 2025, Petitioner, Ronnie Roberts, filed a Charge of
Discrimination with the Florida Commission on Human Relations (“FCHR”),
alleging that Respondent, Miami International Airport (“MIA” or
“Respondent”), unlawfully discriminated against him in a place of public
accommodation by failing to provide him a wheelchair or appropriate seating
while he waited eight hours for a flight on Delta Airlines (“Delta”).
On December 5, 2025, FCHR issued a Notice of Determination to
Petitioner, indicating that FCHR found “no reasonable cause” to believe that
discrimination occurred. Petitioner elected to contest the decision and pursue
administrative remedies by filing a Petition for Relief (“Petition”) with FCHR.
FCHR transmitted the Petition to DOAH on January 6, 2026, and the
undersigned was assigned to hear the case.
The final hearing was held as scheduled on April 8, 2026. At the hearing,
Petitioner testified on his own behalf. He also presented the testimony of
three witnesses: Karen Britton, Petitioner’s wife; Danielle Bishop,
Petitioner’s daughter; and Secolia Bishop, Petitioner’s daughter. Petitioner’s
Exhibits 1 through 34 were admitted.1 Respondent presented the testimony
of Natalie Pavlik, Former Americans with Disabilities Act (“ADA”)
Coordinator for MIA. Respondent’s Exhibits 1 through 7 were admitted into
evidence.
The deadline for submission of proposed recommended orders by the
parties was set for May 15, 2026. Petitioner submitted a letter summarizing
his argument, and MIA timely submitted a Proposed Recommended Order,
both of which were given consideration in the preparation of this
1 Respondent agreed to admit all of Petitioner’s Exhibits 1 through 34. However, Petitioner
did not submit Exhibits 15 and 31 onto the docket, and, therefore, they were not considered.
2

Recommended Order. Except as otherwise indicated, citations to Florida
Statutes refer to the 2024 version in effect at the time of the alleged violation.
FINDINGS OF FACT
The Parties
1. MIA2 is a Department of Miami-Dade County, Florida, which is a
political subdivision of the State of Florida charged with operating a local
government within the geographic boundaries of Miami-Dade County,
Florida.
2. Petitioner, Ronnie Roberts, is a 61-year-old individual who has multiple
documented physical disabilities, including a neurological seizure disorder,
and history of multiple knee, back, and leg surgeries, which limit his
mobility. He regularly uses a walker and/or cane for ambulation.
The September 20, 2024, Incident
3. On September 20, 2024, Petitioner arrived at MIA at approximately
10:00 a.m. with his wife, Karen Britton, his stepdaughters, Danielle Bishop
and Secolia Bishop, and his four-year-old granddaughter. The family had
returned from a birthday cruise and was departing on a Delta flight to
Raleigh-Durham, North Carolina, scheduled for approximately 6:30 p.m. that
evening.
4. Petitioner did not bring his walker or cane to the airport. However,
Petitioner’s disability was visibly apparent through his physical condition,
use of mobility aids, and disability indicators, including the use of a
sunflower lanyard.3
2 Respondent refers to itself in its Proposed Recommended Order as Miami-Dade County
Aviation Department. This is inconsistent with how Respondent was identified throughout
the FCHR process and the style of the case. Accordingly, the undersigned is referring to
Respondent as MIA.
3 A sunflower lanyard is a globally recognized symbol used to discreetly indicate that the
wearer has a hidden, non-visible disability. It alerts staff and the public that the wearer may
need extra time, assistance, or simply more understanding. They are provided free at the
information desk in many major airports or may be purchased online.
3

5. Upon arriving at the airport, Petitioner and his family asked various
individuals within the terminal about wheelchair assistance. The individuals
they approached consistently directed them to Delta as the party responsible
for providing wheelchair services.
6. Petitioner and his family eventually located the Delta ticket counter
area. A Delta employee informed the family that wheelchair assistance was
available, but pursuant to Delta’s policy, wheelchair service would escort
Petitioner directly to his gate.
7. Petitioner did not accept the offer of wheelchair escort to his gate.
Instead, Petitioner and his family left for a little while and then decided to
return to the Delta counter to ask if the airport or Delta could loan them a
wheelchair for use around the airport.
8. The Delta agent explained that they could not provide Petitioner with a
wheelchair eight hours before his flight to roam about the airport due to
liability issues and that the airport does not offer wheelchair services.
9. The Delta agent offered Petitioner and his family the seating that was
available near doors 22 and 23, which was across from the Delta ticket
counters. According to Petitioner and his family, multiple cruise ship
passengers arrived at or near the same time and seating in the terminal was
extremely limited with some passengers sitting on the floor.
10. Petitioner’s daughters approached multiple individuals throughout the
terminal regarding wheelchair access. Each individual directed them to the
airline as the responsible party.
11. MIA maintains multiple passenger accessibility reporting channels
throughout its terminals, including posted screens with ADA Coordinator
contact information, QR codes for direct complaint submission, and staffed
information counters. Neither Petitioner nor his family members contacted
MIA’s ADA Coordinator, approached any MIA customer service or
information counter, or utilized any of the MIA accessibility contact resources
posted throughout the terminal on the date of the incident.
4

12. Approximately 35 to 40 minutes after arriving at the airport, when
attempting to use the restroom, Petitioner collapsed on the airport floor, lost
consciousness for about 15 minutes, and was transported by ambulance to
Jackson West Hospital. After being seen and treated in the Emergency Room,
Petitioner returned to the airport. Upon his return, individuals, whom he
assumed were airport employees, provided him wheelchair assistance when
he entered the terminal.
Post-Incident Investigation by MIA
13. Initially, Petitioner characterized the fall as the result of a wet and
slippery substance on the floor. Petitioner’s wife, Ms. Britton, acting on his
behalf, reported to airport personnel that Petitioner had slipped and fallen in
a wet area at MIA. After reaching out to Risk Management and being
redirected to the janitorial company who told Petitioner that they would not
be covering him under their insurance, Petitioner then changed his narrative
and filed a complaint of discrimination based on unlawful public
accommodation practices.4
14. Natalie Pavlik, MIA’s then ADA Coordinator, and current Special
Projects Administrator, investigated Petitioner’s complaint and testified that
MIA’s sole responsibility is to ensure the physical accessibility of its terminal
facilities. Wheelchair assistance to individual passengers is the responsibility
of the air carrier under the Air Carrier Access Act (“ACAA”). MIA does not
employ, supervise, or deploy wheelchair personnel at the airport. Those
individuals are employed by or contracted through the airlines. MIA has not
contractually agreed to provide wheelchair services to any airline’s
passengers.
15. MIA provides accessible seating both at pre-security and post-security
areas of the airport, including near doors 22 and 23 adjacent to the Delta
ticket counters, with additional general seating available immediately
4 Petitioner’s credibility and that of his witnesses was somewhat lessened by this
contradictory explanation of what occurred and why he was injured.
5

adjacent to the designated accessible area. This seating was available and
operational on the date of the incident.
16. Contrary to Petitioner’s allegation that there were no readily available
seats throughout the entire airport, MIA received no complaints, service
requests, or escalations from Petitioner, his family, or any other airport
passengers on the date of the incident. The only MIA record from that date
pertaining to Petitioner is a fire and rescue incident report filed after his fall.
17. Ms. Pavlik reviewed Petitioner’s Exhibit 5, video footage from inside
the terminal where an individual speaks with Petitioner’s daughter, and
testified that the individual depicted is not an MIA employee. Based on the
uniform and logo visible in the footage, the individual is consistent with a
Maximus Global Services employee, a wheelchair contractor employed by
Delta, not MIA.
18. Ms. Pavlik also reviewed Petitioner’s Exhibit 8, video footage from
inside the terminal where an individual directs Petitioner and his family to
the airline for assistance, and testified that the individual depicted wears a
green badge. MIA employees wear blue badges exclusively. A green badge
identifies a contractor, not an MIA employee.
19. Petitioner’s stepdaughter, Ms. Bishop, testified that she assumed
the individuals she encountered were airport employees because they wore
badges. No individual identified themselves as an MIA employee, and
Ms. Bishop could not confirm the employer of any individual beyond the
Delta ticket counter employee. No evidence was presented that demonstrated
Petitioner or his family made any contact with an MIA employee to seek
wheelchair or seating assistance on the date of the incident.
20. Ms. Pavlik explained that if Petitioner or his family had notified an
MIA employee of the need for additional seating, temporary seating could
have been made available immediately.
6

21. The Federal Aviation Administration conducted a compliance audit of
MIA in December 2024, with no findings of non-compliance related to
accessibility programs, services, or physical infrastructure.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
22. DOAH has jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter of this
cause pursuant to sections 120.569, 120.57(1), and 760.11(7), Florida Statutes
(2025).
23. Petitioner alleges that MIA unlawfully discriminated against him on
the basis of disability by failing to provide him a wheelchair and proper
seating. Petitioner contends that, but for Respondent’s failure to provide him
wheelchair or seating, he would not have fallen and suffered injuries,
including worsening pain, increased seizure activity, reduced mobility,
emotional distress, diminished quality of life, and continuing physical
impairment.
Burden of Proof
24. Petitioner has the burden of proving that Respondent failed to provide
full and equal enjoyment of its accommodations on the basis of his handicap.
Fla. Dep’t of Transp. v. J.W.C. Co., 396 So. 2d 778 (Fla. 1st DCA 1981).
Petitioner must prove the elements of public accommodation discrimination
by a preponderance of the evidence. § 120.57(1)(j), Fla. Stat.; see Young v.
Dep’t of Cmty. Aff., 625 So. 2d 831 (Fla. 1993).
Public Accommodation Discrimination
25. The FCRA is codified at sections 760.01 through 760.11. Section
760.08, titled “Discrimination in places of public accommodation,” states:
“[a]ll persons are entitled to the full and equal enjoyment of the goods,
services, facilities, privileges, advantages, and accommodations of any place
of public accommodation without discrimination or segregation on the ground
of race, color, national origin, sex, pregnancy, handicap, familial status, or
7

religion.” This provision prohibits discrimination against protected classes,
including handicapped persons, in places of public accommodation.
26. The FCRA defines the term “public accommodations” as “places of
public accommodation, lodgings, facilities principally engaged in selling food
for consumption on the premises, gasoline stations, places of exhibition or
entertainment, and other covered establishments.” § 760.02(11), Fla. Stat.
The statute specifically enumerates certain establishments that qualify as
places of public accommodation, including “any motion picture theater,
theater, concert hall, sports arena, stadium, or other place of exhibition or
entertainment.” Id. Notably, the statutory definition does not expressly
include airports, transportation facilities, or common carriers within the
enumerated categories of public accommodations under the FCRA.
27. Florida courts apply the doctrine of expressio unius est exclusio alterius
when interpreting the FCRA’s definition of public accommodations, meaning
that the Legislature’s inclusion of specific establishments implies the
exclusion of others not listed. Okposio v. Barry Univ., 252 So. 3d 1290, 1292
(Fla. 1st DCA 2018). In Okposio, the court held that despite a university
having libraries or “places of entertainment” on its premises, it was not a
place of public accommodation under the FCRA. Id. at 1291. The court
reasoned that “had the Florida Legislature wished to include such places
within its definition of ‘public accommodations,’ it certainly could have done
so.” Id. at 1292.
28. Airports, which are also not enumerated in section 760.02(11), would
similarly fall outside the FCRA’s definition of public accommodations.
29. Because the FCRA is substantially similar to the ADA, courts construe
the two in conformity. Abadi v. Walt Disney World Parks & Resorts, 338 So.
3d 1101, 1104 (Fla. 1st DCA 2022).
30. To prevail on an ADA public accommodation claim in Florida, a
Petitioner must prove: (1) that Petitioner is disabled within the meaning of
the ADA; (2) that Respondent owns, leases, or operates a place of public
8

accommodation; and (3) that Respondent discriminated against the Petitioner
within the meaning of the ADA. Heimkes v. Fairhope Motorcoach Resort
Condo. Owners Ass’n, Inc., 2026 WL 824959, at *3 (S.D. Ala. Mar. 25, 2026).
See also Kennedy v. Floridian Hotel, Inc., 998 F.3d 1221, 1231 (11th Cir.
2021) (applying the same factors).
31. Petitioner meets the first prong. His disabilities are documented and
not in dispute. However, his claim fails on the second prong. As explained in
more detail below, MIA does not own, lease, or operate a place of public
accommodation within the meaning of the ADA or the FCRA. Accordingly,
the third prong need not be reached. Even assuming that Petitioner
demonstrated the applicability of the ADA and the FCRA, he does not meet
the third prong because he failed to put forth evidence that any
representative of MIA discriminated against him.
Title II of the ADA Applies to Governmental Entities–Not Title III
32. The ADA is divided into separate titles that govern distinct categories
of entities with distinct legal obligations. “Title I prohibits discrimination in
private employment; Title II prohibits discrimination by public entities; and
Title III prohibits discrimination by a ‘place of public accommodation,’ which
is a private entity that offers commercial services to the public.” A.L. by &
through D.L. v. Walt Disney Parks & Resorts US, Inc., 900 F.3d 1270, 1289
(11th Cir. 2018). This structural distinction is dispositive of Petitioner’s
claim.
33. Title II of the ADA applies to public entities, state and local
governments and their agencies and instrumentalities. 42 U.S.C. § 12132.
MIA, as a department of Miami-Dade County, is a public entity subject to
Title II of the ADA, not Title III.
34. Title III of the ADA applies to places of public accommodation
operated by private entities. 42 U.S.C. § 12182(a). Title III expressly excludes
facilities covered by Title II from its public accommodation provisions.
42 U.S.C. § 12181. Because MIA is a governmental airport operator subject to
9

Title II, Title III does not apply, and Petitioner cannot maintain a Title III
public accommodation claim against MIA.
35. Title II obligations attach to the services and programs the public
entity itself controls and operates. 42 U.S.C. § 12132. Specifically, in this
case, the ACAA has expressly assigned responsibility for wheelchair service
to Delta. Therefore, a Title II claim against MIA for that same service cannot
stand. The wheelchair assistance Petitioner sought is a service the law
assigns to the airlines, not to MIA. See 14 C.F.R. § 382.91.
36. Even if MIA were a private entity potentially covered by Title III,
airport terminals are not included within the enumerated categories of places
of public accommodation under Title III. 42 U.S.C. § 12181(7). Title III of the
ADA prohibits discrimination in public accommodations, commercial
facilities, and specified public transportation. 42 U.S.C. § 12181. Under this
framework, a “public accommodation” includes “a terminal, depot, or other
station used for specified public transportation.” See 42 U.S.C. § 12181(7)(G).
The statute defines “specified public transportation” as “transportation by
bus, rail, or any other conveyance (other than by aircraft) that provides the
general public with general or special service (including charter service) on a
regular and continuing basis.” 42 U.S.C. § 12181(10). Reading these
provisions together, the statutory language is unambiguous and clearly
establishes that airplanes and terminals used for air travel are excluded from
coverage under Title III of the ADA. Mennella v. Am. Airlines, Inc., No. 17-cv-
21915-GAYLES, 2017 WL 6560467, at *2 (S.D. Fla. Dec. 22, 2017). See also
Lopez v. Jet Blue Airways, 662 F.3d 593, 599 (2nd Cir. 2011)( Public
transportation terminals, depots, or stations used primarily to facilitate air
transportation are not “public accommodation[s]” for purposes of Title III of
the ADA.).
37. Accordingly, even under Title III of the ADA, no cognizable public
accommodation claim lies against MIA as the governmental operator of MIA.
10

Air Carrier Access Act
38. The ACAA establishes the comprehensive federal framework
governing disability accommodations in air travel. Under the ACAA, the
obligation to provide wheelchair and mobility assistance to passengers rests
explicitly and exclusively with the air carrier—not the airport operator. 14
C.F.R. § 382.91(a). The air carrier is required to provide wheelchair
assistance to passengers who request it, including assistance through the
terminal, to and from the gate, and during boarding and deplaning. 14 C.F.R.
§ 382.91(b).
39. Title 49 C.F.R. § 27.71 provides that “airport operators shall ensure
that the terminal facilities and services subject to this section shall be readily
accessible to and usable by individuals with disabilities, including individuals
who use wheelchairs.” 49 C.F.R. § 27.71(b). Airport operators are in
compliance with this statute if they meet requirements applying to state and
local government programs or activities and facilities under Department of
Justice (DOJ) regulations implementing Title II of the ADA. Id.
40. An air carrier and airport operator may contract to delegate these
responsibilities. 49 C.F.R. § 27.71(f). Contracts or leases between carriers and
airport operators concerning the use of airport facilities must set forth the
respective responsibilities of the parties for the provision of accessible
facilities and services to individuals with disabilities for carriers. Id. Simply
put, airports receiving federal financial assistance have specific
responsibilities to ensure accessibility for individuals with disabilities,
including maintaining accessible paths between gates and aircraft boarding
areas, establishing clear contractual responsibilities with carriers, and
submitting transition plans for existing facilities.
41. Here, MIA has not contractually assumed any obligation to provide
wheelchair services to any airline’s passengers. Ms. Pavlik testified without
contradiction that MIA does not employ, supervise, or deploy the personnel
who provide wheelchair assistance to passengers at the airport. Those
11

individuals are employed by or contracted through the airlines—in this case,
Delta, through its contractor, MGS. An airport operator may assume
additional responsibilities through contract, but no such contract exists here.
42. The accommodation Petitioner sought, wheelchair assistance and
seating, was offered by Delta through its contractor, MGS, consistent with
the airline’s obligations under the ACAA. That offer included a direct escort
to Petitioner’s gate and seating near the ticket counter. Petitioner declined
the offer. A party who is offered the precise accommodation the law requires
and declines that offer cannot subsequently maintain that the
accommodation was denied. Bryant v. Caritas Norwood Hosp., 345 F. Supp.
2d 155, 168 (D. Mass. 2004).
Conclusion
43. Although Petitioner undoubtedly sustained significant injuries at
MIA, he failed to demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that he
was entitled to, and was denied, reasonable accommodations from MIA, or
that he is entitled to any damages recoverable against this Respondent
pursuant to the FCRA.
RECOMMENDATION
Based on the foregoing Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, it is
RECOMMENDED that the Florida Commission on Human Relations issue a
final order finding that Petitioner, Ronnie Roberts, did not prove that
Respondent, Miami International Airport, committed an unlawful public
accommodation practice against him, and dismissing his Petition for Relief
from an unlawful public accommodation practice.
12

title: DOAH 26-0053 Recommended Order: KALIYAH LANIER vs. LOADING...GASTROBRUNCH
text:
STATE OF FLORIDA
DIVISION OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
KALIYAH LANIER,
Petitioner,
vs. Case No. 26-0053
MJ2 LLC D/B/A
LOADING...GASTROBRUNCH,
Respondent.
/
RECOMMENDED ORDER
Pursuant to notice, a final hearing was conducted on May 5, 2026, via
Zoom teleconference, before Linzie F. Bogan, a duly-designated
Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) of the Division of Administrative Hearings
(DOAH).
APPEARANCES
For Petitioner: Kaliyah Sharnell Lanier, pro se
5020 West Irlo Bronson Memorial Highway
Kissimmee, Florida 34746
For Respondent: No one appeared
STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES
Whether Respondent, MJ2 LLC d/b/a Loading…Gastrobrunch
(Respondent or MJ2), subjected Petitioner to discrimination on the basis of
her race in violation of section 760.10, Florida Statutes, and whether
Respondent retaliated against Petitioner for the exercise of protected rights
under section 760.10.1
1 All references to the Florida Statutes are to the 2025 version unless otherwise noted.

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
On May 30, 2025, Petitioner, Kaliyah Lanier (Petitioner), filed with the
Florida Commission on Human Relations (FCHR) a Complaint of
Employment Discrimination alleging that Respondent discriminated against
her based on her race and color, and retaliated against her for the exercise of
protected rights. FCHR investigated the allegations. On November 25, 2025,
FCHR issued a written determination that there was no reasonable cause to
believe that an unlawful practice occurred.
On or about December 21, 2025, Petitioner timely filed a Petition for
Relief with FCHR. On January 6, 2026, FCHR referred the case to DOAH for
the assignment of an ALJ so that a final hearing could be held. The final
hearing was convened on March 5, 2026. Petitioner appeared for the final
hearing but no one appeared on behalf of Respondent.
On March 5, 2026, an Order Regarding Proper Respondent was entered,
in part, because information provided by FCHR to DOAH did not properly
identify Respondent. Per the Order, Respondent’s three managers and its
registered agent were provided with notice regarding this matter and the
style of the case was updated to reflect the proper Respondent. The case was
continued, sue sponte, and the final hearing was rescheduled for May 5, 2026.
As noted in the Order Regarding Proper Respondent, Jahnae Allen is
listed as a “manager” for Respondent with the Florida Department of State.
Notice of the final hearing scheduled for May 5, 2026, was mailed to
Ms. Allen at the address on file with the Department of State, and the same
was returned to DOAH as undeliverable and the envelope containing the
notice was marked as “vacant” by the United States Postal Service (USPS).
None of the other notices mailed on March 31, 2026, to Respondent’s
2

registered agent and two other managers regarding the rescheduled hearing
were returned to DOAH by USPS.
Petitioner testified on her own behalf and called no other witnesses.
Petitioner’s two Exhibits were admitted into evidence. Neither party filed a
transcript of the final hearing nor submitted a proposed recommended order.
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. From February 14, 2025, until May 11, 2025, Petitioner worked for
Respondent as a table busser. Petitioner’s job responsibilities included
clearing and resetting dining room tables, assisting servers, maintaining the
cleanliness of the dining room, and other related functions. According to
Petitioner, she normally worked about 25 hours per week for Respondent,
earned $12.00 per hour, and averaged about $50.00 per week in tips.
2. In April 2025, Respondent “drastically reduced” Petitioner’s work hours
and scheduled her to work “only one shift for the entire” month. Although the
exact date is unclear, Petitioner, at some point, complained to Jahnae Allen,
one of the managers at the restaurant, about her reduced work hours during
April and that she had not been scheduled to work any hours during May.
Respondent did not respond to Petitioner’s complaint.
3. Although Respondent did not schedule Petitioner to work in May,
Respondent contacted Petitioner on May 10, 2025, and offered her a double
shift. Petitioner reported to work, as agreed, and during her shift one of the
managers yelled at Petitioner and accused her of giving free food to
customers. According to Petitioner’s undisputed and credible testimony, a co-
worker “immediately corrected [the manager] and explained that customers
had moved tables on their own and that [Petitioner] had done nothing
wrong.”
4. At 4:11 a.m. on May 11, 2025, Petitioner was included on a group chat
message in which the manager informed Petitioner that her employment was
3

terminated due to reasons related to her work “performance.” Petitioner’s
undisputed and credible testimony was that before the termination of her
employment she had never received any “warnings, write-ups, coaching, or
documentation indicating performance concerns.”
5. Petitioner contends that she was “discriminated and retaliated against
based on [her] darker complexion and for asking about [her] reduced hours to
no hours.” In explaining her allegations, Petitioner testified that her white
co-workers were treated more favorably by Respondent and in support
thereof offered the following examples.
6. First, Petitioner contends that she was disciplined more severely than
her white co-workers. According to Petitioner, a white co-worker named Joy
“seated customers at the Viking table despite being instructed not to use that
table.” Petitioner’s undisputed and credible testimony was that despite the
warning, Joy “was not publicly reprimanded, yelled at, or addressed in the
group chat.”
7. Second, Petitioner contends that she was excluded from membership in
the “OG” workgroup. This group consisted of white individuals who were
apparently original employees of the restaurant. According to Petitioner, the
use of the term “OG” “felt racially charged rather than accidental.”
8. Finally, Petitioner, in support of her claim, testified that “[o]ther
employees openly stated in the group chat that they were running late [for
work], [and] no public reprimand” was issued to them by Respondent.
Petitioner did not present evidence that she was disciplined for reporting late
to work while her white co-workers were not.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
9. DOAH has jurisdiction of the subject matter of and the parties to this
proceeding. §§ 120.569, 120.57(1), and 760.11(7), Fla. Stat.
4

10. The Florida Civil Rights Act of 1992 (Florida Civil Rights Act or the
FCRA), chapter 760, prohibits discrimination in the workplace. The FCRA is
modeled after Title VII of the Civil Rights Acts of 1964 and 1991, 42 U.S.C.
§ 2000, et seq. (Title VII), so that federal case law regarding Title VII is
applicable to construe the FCRA. See Castleberry v. Edward M. Chadbourne,
Inc., 810 So. 2d 1028, 1030 (Fla. 1st DCA 2002).
11. Section 760.10 states the following:
(1) It is an unlawful employment practice for an
employer:
(a) To discharge or to fail or refuse to hire any
individual, or otherwise to discriminate against any
individual with respect to compensation, terms,
conditions, or privileges of employment, because of
such individual's race, color, religion, sex, national
origin, age, handicap, or marital status.
* * *
(7) It is an unlawful employment practice for an
employer, an employment agency, a joint labor
management committee, or a labor organization to
discriminate against any person because that person
has opposed any practice which is an unlawful
employment practice under this section, or because
that person has made a charge, testified, assisted, or
participated in any manner in an investigation,
proceeding, or hearing under this section.
12. Respondent does not dispute that it is an “employer” as defined in
section 760.02(7), which provides the following:
“Employer” means any person employing 15 or more
employees for each working day in each of 20 or more
calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar
year, and any agent of such a person.
13. Florida courts have determined that federal case law applies to claims
arising under the Florida Civil Rights Act, and as such, the United States
Supreme Court’s model for employment discrimination cases set forth in
5

McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973), applies to claims
arising under section 760.10, absent direct evidence of discrimination. See
Harper v. Blockbuster Ent. Corp., 139 F.3d 1385, 1387 (11th Cir. 1998);
Paraohao v. Bankers Club, Inc., 225 F. Supp. 2d 1353, 1361 (S.D. Fla. 2002);
Fla. State Univ. v. Sondel, 685 So. 2d 923, 925 n.1 (Fla. 1st DCA 1996); Fla.
Dep’t of Cmty. Aff. v. Bryant, 586 So. 2d 1205 (Fla. 1st DCA 1991).
14. “Direct evidence is ‘evidence, which if believed, proves existence of fact
in issue without inference or presumption.’” Rollins v. TechSouth, Inc., 833
F.2d 1525, 1528 n.6 (11th Cir. 1987) (quoting Black’s Law Dictionary 413 (5th
ed. 1979)). In Carter v. City of Miami, 870 F.2d 578, 582 (11th Cir. 1989), the
court stated:
This Court has held that not every comment
concerning a person's age presents direct evidence of
discrimination. [Young v. Gen. Foods Corp., 840 F.2d
825, 829 (11th Cir. 1988)]. The Young Court made
clear that remarks merely referring to
characteristics associated with increasing age, or
facially neutral comments from which a plaintiff has
inferred discriminatory intent, are not directly
probative of discrimination. Id. Rather, courts have
found only the most blatant remarks, whose intent
could be nothing other than to discriminate on the
basis of age, to constitute direct evidence of
discrimination.
15. Petitioner offered no evidence that would satisfy the stringent
standard of direct evidence of discrimination.
16. Under the McDonnell analysis, in employment discrimination cases,
Petitioner has the burden of establishing, by a preponderance of evidence, a
prima facie case of unlawful discrimination. If the prima facie case is
established, the burden shifts to the employer to rebut this preliminary
showing by producing evidence that the adverse action was taken for some
legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason. If the employer rebuts the prima facie
case, the burden shifts back to Petitioner to show by a preponderance of the
6

evidence that the employer’s offered reasons for its adverse employment
decision were pretextual. See Tex. Dep’t of Cmty. Aff. v. Burdine, 450 U.S. 248
(1981).
17. To prove a prima facie case of unlawful employment discrimination
under chapter 760, Petitioner must establish that: (1) she is a member of the
protected group; (2) she was subject to adverse employment action; (3)
Respondent treated similarly situated employees outside of her protected
classifications more favorably; and (4) Petitioner was qualified to do the job
and was performing her job at a level that met the employer’s legitimate
expectations. See, e.g., Jiles v. United Parcel Serv., Inc., 360 Fed. Appx. 61, 64
(11th Cir. 2010); Burke-Fowler v. Orange Cnty., 447 F.3d 1319, 1323 (11th
Cir. 2006); Knight v. Baptist Hosp. of Miami, Inc., 330 F.3d 1313, 1316 (11th
Cir. 2003); Williams v. Vitro Servs. Corp., 144 F.3d 1438, 1441 (11th Cir.
1998); McKenzie v. EAP Mgmt. Corp., 40 F. Supp. 2d 1369, 1374-75 (S.D. Fla.
1999).
18. Petitioner has not established a prima facie case of unlawful
employment discrimination.
19. The undisputed evidence demonstrated Petitioner is an African-
American female and is therefore a member of a protected group.
20. The undisputed evidence demonstrated Petitioner was fired from her
position with MJ2 and was therefore subject to an adverse employment
action.
21. Petitioner was qualified to hold the “busser” position at MJ2, and
Petitioner’s undisputed evidence is that she was performing her job at a level
at or above expectations.
22. As to the question of disparate treatment, the applicable standard was
recently revised in Lewis v. City of Union City, Georgia, 918 F.3d 1213, 1218
(11th Cir. 2019): “[A] plaintiff asserting an intentional-discrimination claim
under McDonnell-Douglas must demonstrate that she and her proffered
comparators were ‘similarly situated in all material aspects.’”
7

23. State courts in Florida have found that a person suffers “disparate
treatment” in his or her employment, in violation of Title VII—and, by
extension, the FCRA—when he or she is singled out and treated less
favorably on the basis of his or her status as a member of a protected class
than other employees who are otherwise similarly situated in all relevant
respects. Johnson v. Great Expressions Dental Ctrs. of Fla., P.A., 132 So. 3d
1174, 1176 (Fla. 3d DCA 2014); Valenzuela v. Globeground N. Am., LLC, 18
So. 3d 17, 23 (Fla. 3d DCA 2009).
24. Petitioner offered no evidence as to the disparate treatment of
similarly situated employees outside of her protected classification.
Specifically, Petitioner did not present evidence that similarly situated white
employees were not also terminated by group chat, or that white individuals
remained employed at MJ2 despite being accused of giving free food to
customers.
25. While it is undisputed that her work hours were reduced during April
and May, Petitioner presented no evidence that the work hours of similarly
situated white bussers remained unchanged during this period.
26. Discriminatory intent may be proved by inference, but a trier of fact
“cannot infer discrimination from thin air.” Lizardo v. Denny’s, Inc., 270 F.3d
94, 104 (2d Cir. 2001), citing Norton v. Sam’s Club, 145 F.3d 114, 119 (2d
Cir.1998). Mere speculation or self-serving belief on the part of a complainant
concerning motives of a respondent is insufficient, standing alone, to
establish a prima facie case of intentional discrimination. See Lizardo, 270
F.3d at 104 (“Plaintiffs have done little more than cite to their mistreatment
and ask the court to conclude that it must have been related to their race.
This is not sufficient.”). See also Norton, 145 F.3d at 120 (anti-discrimination
law “does not make employers liable for doing stupid or even wicked things; it
makes them liable for discriminating….”). (emphasis added).
27. While Petitioner may have experienced less than desirable treatment
while employed at MJ2, the evidence is insufficient to reasonably infer that
8

any perceived or actual difference in treatment was as a result of illegal,
discriminatory animus. Petitioner failed to prove disparate treatment based
on her race.
28. As to Petitioner’s retaliation claim, the court in Blizzard v. Appliance
Direct, Inc., 16 So. 3d 922, 926 (Fla. 5th DCA 2009), described the elements of
such a claim as follows:
To establish a prima facie case of retaliation under
section 760.10(7), a plaintiff must demonstrate:
(1) that he or she engaged in statutorily protected
activity; (2) that he or she suffered adverse
employment action; and (3) that the adverse
employment action was causally related to the
protected activity. See Harper v. Blockbuster Entm’t
Corp., 139 F.3d 1385, 1388 (11th Cir.), cert. denied
525 U.S. 1000, 119 S. Ct. 509, 142 L.Ed.2d 422
(1998). Once the plaintiff makes a prima facie
showing, the burden shifts and the defendant must
articulate a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for
the adverse employment action. Wells v. Colorado
Dep't of Transp., 325 F.3d 1205, 1212 (10th Cir.
2003). The plaintiff must then respond by
demonstrating that defendant's asserted reasons for
the adverse action are pretextual. Id.
29. Petitioner made no evidentiary showing that any employment or
postemployment action by Respondent was causally related to any statutorily
protected activity she took while an employee. Petitioner’s retaliation claim
derives from her contention that MJ2 terminated her employment after she
complained about her reduced work hours. Perhaps a reduction in work hours
could support a retaliation claim, see, e.g., Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission v. White and Sons Enterprises, 881 F.2d 1006 (11th Cir. 1989),
but such is not the case herein. Petitioner’s complaint about reduced work
hours, without connecting or otherwise tethering her concern to how the work
hours of similarly situated white employees remained uncut, merely reduces
her complaint to nothing more than an employee grievance that fails to rise
to the level of being statutorily protected activity. In other words, Petitioner
9

did not engage in statutorily protected activity when she complained to
Respondent about a reduction of her work hours, and she, therefore, failed to
meet her burden with respect to her claim of unlawful retaliation.
30. In conclusion, Petitioner failed to present a prima facie case of
discrimination based on race or color, and failed to show that her dismissal
from employment by Respondent was in retaliation for her exercise of
protected activity.
RECOMMENDATION
Based on the foregoing Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, it is
RECOMMENDED that the Florida Commission on Human Relations issue a
final order finding that MJ2 LLC d/b/a Loading…Gastrobrunch did not
commit an unlawful employment practice, and dismissing the Petition for
Relief filed in this case.

County, Florida.
