title: DOAH 26-0107 Recommended Order
text:
STATE OF FLORIDA
DIVISION OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
MOORGEN RAVEN GRIFFIN,
Petitioner,
vs. Case No. 26-0107
FLORIDA DEPARTMENT OF
HEALTH, BOARD OF NURSING
Respondent.
/
RECOMMENDED ORDER
Pursuant to notice, a final hearing was held in this case on March 27,
2026, via Zoom conferencing, before James H. Peterson, III, a designated
Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) with the Division of Administrative
Hearings (DOAH).
APPEARANCES
For Petitioner: Moorgen Raven Griffin, pro se
1105 Ashley Avenue
Indian Harbour Beach, Florida 32937
For Respondent: Deborah Bartholow Loucks, Esquire
Hugh Michael Farnsworth, Esquire
Office of the Attorney General
The Capitol, PL-01
Tallahassee, Florida 32399-1050
STATEMENT OF THE ISSUE
Whether Petitioner should be allowed to take the NCLEX-PN exam as an
equivalent pathway to obtain a practical nursing license based on his petition
for a hardship waiver.

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
On June 26, 2025, Moorgen Raven Griffin (Petitioner) filed a Petition for
Hardship Variance concerning sections 464.008(1)(c) and 464.019(1)(f-g),
Florida Statutes,1 with the Florida Board of Nursing (Respondent or Board).
On August 7, 2025, the Board reviewed and preliminarily denied Petitioner’s
Petition for Hardship Variance on the grounds that Petitioner failed to
demonstrate that he met the purposes of the underlying statute by other
means, and failed to demonstrate how application of rule provisions would
violate principles of fairness or constitute an undue hardship on Petitioner.
On September 10, 2025, the Board’s executive director signed a Notice of
Intent to Deny Petition for Waiver and Variance (Notice). The Notice, filed
with the Florida Department of Health on September 12, 2026, set forth the
reasons for the Board’s denial of the Petitioner’s Petition for Hardship
Variance and advised Petitioner of his right to file a petition for an
administrative hearing within 21 days from receipt of the Notice. On
September 12, 2025, Petitioner timely filed a Petition for Administrative
Hearing, and the matter was forwarded to DOAH, where the matter was
assigned to the undersigned and scheduled for hearing.
At the March 27, 2026, hearing, Petitioner testified on his own behalf and
offered one exhibit, received into evidence as Petitioner’s Exhibit 1.
Respondent presented the testimony of Sherri Sutton-Johnson, DrPH, MSN,
BSN, who was accepted as an expert witness in the educational requirements
for licensure as a licensed practical nurse (LPN). Respondent offered three
exhibits, received into evidence as Respondent’s Exhibits 1 through 3.
1 References to Florida Statutes and Florida Administrative Code Rules are to current
versions.
2

The proceedings were recorded and a transcript was ordered. By
agreement, the parties were given 30 days from the filing of the Transcript
within which to file their proposed recommended orders. The one-volume
Transcript was filed on April 13, 2026. The parties timely filed their
respective Proposed Recommended Orders, both of which have been
considered in the preparation of this Recommended Order.
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. Respondent is the state agency responsible for licensing nurses in the
State of Florida, pursuant to chapter 464.
2. Petitioner attended Horizon Healthcare’s Practical Nursing Program
but did not graduate from that program.
3. Petitioner is currently enrolled in a practical nursing program at
Eastern Florida State College and, when complete, will graduate with a
practical nursing degree.
4. A person applying for nurse licensure may apply to become a practical
nurse (PN) or a professional nurse (RN). Practice as a PN2 differs from
practice as an RN.3 A PN covers basic bedside care and requires a shorter
2 As defined in section 464.003(18):
“Practice of practical nursing” means the performance of selected acts,
including the administration of treatments and medications, in the care of the
ill, injured, or infirm; the promotion of wellness, maintenance of health, and
prevention of illness of others under the direction of a registered nurse, a
licensed physician, a licensed osteopathic physician, a licensed podiatric
physician, or a licensed dentist; and the teaching of general principles of health
and wellness to the public and to students other than nursing students. A
practical nurse is responsible and accountable for making decisions that are
based upon the individual’s educational preparation and experience in
nursing.
3 With regard to an RN, section 464.003(19) provides:
“Practice of professional nursing” means the performance of those acts
requiring substantial specialized knowledge, judgment, and nursing skill
based upon applied principles of psychological, biological, physical, and social
sciences which shall include, but not be limited to:
3

technical program, while an RN involves a broader scope of practice,
including complex clinical assessment and leadership, as well as autonomous
practice.
5. There are two separate National Council Licensure Examination
(NCLEX) examinations for nurses—one for practical nurses (NCLEX-PN) and
one for professional nurses (NCLEX-RN).
6. To obtain a license as a PN, a person must meet the requirements set
out in section 464.008(1)(c), which include: being in good physical and mental
health; having a high school diploma or its equivalent; graduating from an
approved nursing program; passing the NCLEX-PN; and having the ability to
communicate in English.
7. In Florida, there is only one licensure pathway for a student whose
nursing education is only from a practical nursing program. And that is
graduation from an approved practical nursing program and passage of the
NCLEX-PN.
8. Florida law makes an exception under section 464.008(1)(c) for a person
to sit for the NCLEX-PN who has not graduated from an approved practical
nursing program but has attended approved professional nursing (RN)
educational courses and completed a majority of the requirements for
graduation from an RN program. This alternate pathway to licensure testing
pathway is called practical nurse equivalency (PNEQ) because it is based on
the idea that the student who has attended and completed RN educational
(a) The observation, assessment, nursing diagnosis, planning, intervention,
and evaluation of care; health teaching and counseling of the ill, injured, or
infirm; and the promotion of wellness, maintenance of health, and prevention
of illness of others.
(b) The administration of medications and treatments as prescribed or
authorized by a duly licensed practitioner authorized by the laws of this state
to prescribe such medications and treatments.
(c) The supervision and teaching of other personnel in the theory and
performance of any of the acts described in this subsection.
4

courses has educational and clinical experience comparable (or equivalent) to
that of a practical nurse.
9. In this case, Petitioner argues that he has the equivalent education to
become a PN because he has completed most of the practical nursing
educational requirements, obtained additional certifications, and has
healthcare experience outside of his nursing program. There is no evidence,
however, that Petitioner has completed a PN program or a majority of the
requirements for graduation from an RN program.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
10. DOAH has jurisdiction over the parties and subject matter of this
proceeding. § 120.57(1), Fla. Stat.
11. Petitioner carries the ultimate burden of persuasion by a
preponderance of the evidence pursuant to section 120.57(1)(j), to prove that
he meets the statutory requirements to be granted a variance or waiver from
a Board rule.
12. The test as to whether a petition for variance or waiver should be grated
is set forth in section 120.542(2), which states:
(2) Variances and waivers shall be granted when the
person subject to the rule demonstrates that the
purpose of the underlying statute will be or has been
achieved by other means by the person and when
application of a rule would create a substantial
hardship or would violate principles of fairness. For
purposes of this section, “substantial hardship”
means a demonstrated economic, technological,
legal, or other type of hardship to the person
requesting the variance or waiver. For purposes of
this section, “principles of fairness” are violated
when the literal application of a rule affects a
particular person in a manner significantly different
from the way it affects other similarly situated
persons who are subject to the rule.
5

13. A plain reading of the above-quoted statute makes it clear that, under
the statute, variances or waivers can only be granted to requirements of rules
adopted by the agency, not statutes. In the instant case, Petitioner did not
seek a variance from any Board rule. Rather, he seeks a variance or waiver
from the provisions of sections 464.008(1)(c)(which sets forth requirements
for licensure) and 464.019(1)(f-g)(which sets forth curriculum requirements
for practical and professional nursing programs).
14. Section 120.542, Florida Statutes, does not allow an agency to grant a
variance or waiver from a statutory requirement. Because Petitioner did not
request a variance from any Board rule, the Board’s denial of his petition was
correct and should be upheld.
15. In the instant case, Petitioner, in essence, asserts that the underlying
purpose of the statute (section 464.008) would be achieved by allowing him to
qualify to take the NCLEX-PN based upon his healthcare work experience as
a certified nursing assistant and as a registered behavioral technician, and
the practical nursing education that he has completed. This assertion
contradicts the statute. For practical nursing students, they must graduate
from an approved practical nursing program in order to be deemed eligible to
sit for the NCLEX-PN.
16. Further language in section 120.542 addresses whether application of
a rule would create a substantial hardship or would violate principles of
fairness. Petitioner failed to cite any rule from which he is seeking a
variance; he only complained of statutory requirements. The licensing
requirements are set forth in statute and apply to all applicants equally.
17. The hardships cited by Petitioner included additional time to complete
his nursing education and financial considerations. Regardless of those
assertions, the Board does not have the discretion or authority to deviate
from the licensure provisions set forth in the statute so it cannot grant the
relief that Petitioner is seeking through his variance and waiver petition.
6

18. Petitioner does not meet the statutory requirements for the PNEQ
because he has never been enrolled in a professional nursing degree program.
Rather, he has been enrolled in two separate practical nurse programs. As set
forth in the last paragraph of section 464.008(c), the equivalency exception is
for professional nursing (RN) students, not PN students. That last paragraph
of section 464.008(1)(c) states:
Courses successfully completed in a professional
nursing [RN] education program that are at least
equivalent to a practical nursing [PN] education
program may be used to satisfy the education
requirements for licensure as a licensed practical
nurse.
19. The only rule cited by Petitioner is Florida Administrative Code Rule
64B9-3.002, titled Qualification for Examination, which provides:
(3) For an applicant writing the examination for
practical nurses on the basis of practical nursing
education equivalency, a completed Practical Nurse
Equivalence (PNEQ) Application Letter or an official
certified transcript which sets forth graduation from
an approved professional program. The form is
available from the Board office or on the Board’s
website:http:floridasnursing.gov.
20. In sum, as a PN student, not an RN student, by statute (not rule), the
only pathway for licensure available to Petitioner would be to graduate from
an approved PN program and apply to take the NCLEX-PN. A PN student
cannot use training or experience obtained outside of PN school to qualify to
sit for the NCLEX-PN. Rather, the licensing provisions in section 464.008(c)
require that, unless the applicant has qualifying equivalent RN program
credits, the applicant must graduate from a PN program. There is no
statutory or rule authority that would allow applicants for PNEQ to use work
experience, other certifications, or military experience.
7

21. In other words, Petitioner has failed to prove that he should be
allowed to take the NCLEX-PN exam as an equivalent pathway to obtain a
practical nursing license based on his petition for a hardship waiver.
RECOMMENDATION
Based on the foregoing, it is RECOMMENDED that the Board enter a
Final Order denying Petitioner’s Petition for Hardship Variance.

title: DOAH 26-0114TTS Recommended Order: POLK COUNTY SCHOOL BOARD vs. THOMAS GRIFFIN
text:
STATE OF FLORIDA
DIVISION OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
POLK COUNTY SCHOOL BOARD,
Petitioner,
vs. Case No. 26-0114TTS
THOMAS GRIFFIN,
Respondent.
/
RECOMMENDED ORDER
The final hearing in this matter was conducted before Lynne A. Quimby-
Pennock, Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) of the Division of Administrative
Hearings (DOAH), pursuant to sections 120.569 and 120.57(1), Florida
Statutes (2025), on February 27, 2026, by Zoom video conference, from
Tallahassee, Florida.
APPEARANCES
For Petitioner: David R. Carmichael, Esquire
Boswell & Dunlap, LLP
245 Central Avenue
Bartow, Florida 33830
For Respondent: Anthony R. Duran, Jr., Esquire
Tison & Duran, P.A.
9312 North Armenia Avenue
Tampa, Florida 33612
STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES
Whether just cause exists for Petitioner, the Polk County School Board
(the School Board), to discipline Respondent, Thomas B. Griffin, and, if so,
whether termination of Respondent’s employment is the appropriate
discipline.

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
On December 19, 2025, Brian Warren, the Associate Superintendent Chief
of Labor and Employee Relations, issued a letter to Respondent. This letter
reminded Mr. Griffin that he remained on “unpaid Suspension, continuing
[his] status from January 29, 2025, … based on alleged violations of Polk
County School Board Policies, including but not limited to, 3121.01-
Background Screening and Employment History Checks and 3210 –
Standards of Ethical Conduct.” This letter also provided that Superintendent
Frederick R. Heid would recommend to the School Board that Mr. Griffin’s
employment with the School Board be terminated effective January 28, 2026.
On December 23, 2025, Respondent, through his attorney, timely
requested a formal appeal hearing challenging the proposed termination of
his employment. On January 8, 2026, the School Board submitted a request
to DOAH for assignment of an ALJ to “hear a teacher termination case.”
Following receipt of a Joint Response to Initial Order, the Zoom hearing
was scheduled for February 27, 2026, and completed on that date. The
parties filed a Joint Pre-Hearing Stipulation that identified limited facts for
which the parties agreed no evidence would be required at hearing. Those
facts are incorporated into the Findings of Fact to the extent relevant and
identified as such with an “*.”
At the final hearing, the School Board presented the testimony of
Laura McCabe and Brian Warren. The School Board’s Exhibits 1 and 3
2

through 13 were admitted into evidence without objection.1 The School
Board’s Exhibit 2 was admitted over objection. Mr. Griffin testified on his
own behalf, and his Exhibits 1 and 2 were admitted into evidence without
objection.
At the close of the hearing, the parties were advised of and agreed to the
ten-day timeframe to file their post-hearing submittals following DOAH’s
receipt of the hearing transcript. On March 6, 2026, the transcript was
electronically filed at DOAH. A Notice on Proposed Recommended Orders
issued which provided that the “proposed recommended orders (PROs) must
be filed with DOAH no later than the close of business (5:00 p.m.) on Monday,
March 16, 2026.”
Both parties timely filed PROs, which were duly considered in preparing
this Recommended Order. To the extent there were facts or information that
were not presented under oath and subjected to cross-examination during the
hearing, those matters have been excluded from consideration.
In making the findings below, the undersigned only considered hearsay
evidence that supplemented or explained other evidence or would be
admissible over objection in civil actions. § 120.57(1)(c), Fla. Stat. Unless
stated otherwise, all statutory references shall be to that version of the
Florida Statutes in effect at the time of the allegations.
1 Petitioner’s Index listed the Exhibits in numerical order. However, the Exhibits uploaded to
the Exhibit portal do not correspond with the descriptive names given. Specifically, on the
Index, Petitioner’s Exhibit 4 is identified as “Copies of all deposition statement; [pages] 27 -
30.” The documentation appears to be the criminal case docket. There are no deposition
statements. And, although admitted, there are no documents uploaded in Petitioner’s
Exhibits 7 through 12.
3

FINDINGS OF FACT
Based on the credibility of the witnesses who testified, the documentary
evidence admitted at the hearing, and the parties’ stipulations, the following
Findings of Fact are made:
1. The School Board is the duly-constituted governing body charged with
the duty to operate, control, and supervise public schools in Polk County,
Florida. See Art. IX, § 4(b), Fla. Const.; and §§ 1001.30 and 1001.33, Fla. Stat.
Witnesses and Duties
2. *Respondent is a teacher employed by the School Board, working under
the School Board and the Polk Education Association, Inc.’s, Teacher
Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA). Mr. Griffin worked with students
with disabilities as a full-time math teacher.
3. Brian Warren is currently employed by the School Board as the chief of
labor and employee relations. Mr. Warren oversees all of the School Board’s
contract negotiations and disciplines. Mr. Warren was the Associate
Superintendent or Chief of the School Board’s Human Resource Services
(HRS) in 2024.
4. Laura McCabe is the Director of Labor and Employee Relations in HRS
for the School Board. Ms. McCabe is responsible for mainly Level 2
background screening handling the fingerprint background checks, long
medical leaves of absence, collective bargaining matters, negotiations, and
contract interpretation. She also supervises the School Board’s investigative
team.
Issue of the Case
5. *Respondent was arrested in mid-December 2024, and charged with
Burglary of a Dwelling (Felony 2d degree), Felony Battery (Felony 3d degree),
and Battery by Strangulation (Felony 3d degree).
6. The School Board was notified of Respondent’s arrest and there was
local newspaper coverage. Although it is speculation on what effect, if any,
the newspaper article(s) might have on any particular population,
4

Mr. Warren was “mindful” that “parents and parents of students” may have
read the stories as he had done.
7. On December 16, 2024, Superintendent Heid placed Respondent on
paid administrative leave (PAL) based on alleged violations of School Board’s
Policy 3210–Standards of Ethical Conduct.
8. Less than a month later on January 10, 2025, Mr. Warren issued a
second letter to Mr. Griffin. This letter advised Mr. Griffin that effective that
day, he was suspended with pay and Superintendent Heid was
recommending Mr. Griffin’s termination of employment with the School
Board. The three criminal charges, all of which were felonies at that time,
were listed in the letter and two of the charges were considered to be
disqualifying offenses. The letter cited section 435.04, Florida Statutes, and
School Board’s Policy 3121.01 for the Superintendent’s decision to
recommend Mr. Griffin’s employment termination. Approximately two weeks
later, Respondent was suspended without pay from his position.
9. On the advice of counsel in October 2025, *Respondent pled to (two
misdemeanor charges: Battery (Misdemeanor lst degree) and Trespass
Structure or Conveyance (Misdemeanor 2d degree) for 12 months’ probation,
adjudication was withheld. In other words, Respondent changed his plea from
not guilty to nolo contendere (commonly referred to as “nolo” or “no contest”)
to two misdemeanor charges): simple battery and trespass.
10. The criminal court withheld the adjudication of guilt and imposed the
following sentence on Respondent: six months’ probation on the Trespass
count, twelve months’ probation on the simple battery count, a fine of
$2,900.00 to be paid to the victim, and an anger management course. The
probation period was allowed to run concurrently. Additionally, Respondent
was not to have contact with the victim, either directly or indirectly through
a third party.
11. *The charge of Battery by Strangulation (Felony 3d degree) was nolle
prossed or dismissed by the State Attorney’s Office.
5

12. Following the conclusion of the criminal case, on December 19, 2025,
Mr. Warren issued another letter to Mr. Griffin. In this letter, Mr. Warren
outlined that Respondent’s PAL was initiated on December 16, 2024;
Respondent’s suspension with pay was initiated on January 10, 2025; and
Respondent’s suspension without pay was effective on January 29, 2025.
13. This December letter also identified Mr. Griffin’s violation of section
435.04 by citing the Level 2 screening standards verbatim:
(2)The security background investigations under
this section must ensure that persons subject to
this section have not been arrested for and are
awaiting final disposition of; have not been found
guilty of, regardless of adjudication, or entered a
plea of nolo contendere or guilty to; or have not
been adjudicated delinquent and the record has not
been sealed or expunged for, any offense prohibited
under any of the following provisions of state law or
similar law of another jurisdiction:
* * *
(k) Chapter 784, relating to assault, battery, and
culpable negligence, if the offense was a felony.
* * *
(r) section 787.02, relating to false imprisonment.
* * *
(hh) section 810.02, relating to burglary.
14. Additionally, this December letter included information that
Superintendent Heid considered regarding Mr. Griffin’s pattern of
indiscretions since 2007. Mr. Griffin was arrested in November 2007 and
January 2015, was given a three-day unpaid suspension in March 2015, and
arrested in June 2017.2 In October 2017, the Florida Department of
2 The outcome of any of the arrests between 2007 and 2017 were not disclosed.
6

Education (FDOE) issued a “Sanction and Reprimand” to Mr. Griffin. Finally,
the three arrests addressed in this Order, prompted FDOE to open an
investigation of Mr. Griffin.
15. Ms. McCabe credibly testified that she serves as a “resource liaison” to
FDOE. Should an FDOE investigator reach out during its investigation,
Ms. McCabe will assist FDOE by giving the investigator what is needed and
coordinate with the appropriate personnel. However, as of the hearing, she
was unaware of the status of the FDOE investigation.
16. Mr. Griffin postulated his belief that the two misdemeanors he pled to
would “absolutely not” affect his ability to teach students.
17. Mr. Warren credibly testified that when someone is charged with
certain enumerated felonies, the School Board needs to evaluate the charges
which could render an employee ineligible for employment.
18. The December 2025 letter discussed in paragraphs 12 through 14
above, then specifically identified the School Board policies Superintendent
Heid utilized for his recommendation to terminate Mr. Griffin’s employment.
Included in the list are: School Board policies 3120; 3210; and 3231, which
will be provided below.
19. Based on the evidence and testimony adduced during the final
hearing, the School Board proved, by a preponderance of the evidence, that
Respondent’s actions violated School Board policies. Accordingly, “just cause”
exists, pursuant to section 1012.33(1)(a), Florida Statutes, for the School
Board to terminate Respondent’s employment.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
20. DOAH has jurisdiction over the subject matter and parties to this
proceeding pursuant to sections 120.569, 120.57(1), and 1012.33(6)(a)2.
21. The School Board is the duly-constituted governing body of the School
District of Polk County. Art. IX, § 4, Fla. Const.; §§ 1001.30 and 1001.33, Fla.
Stat. A district school board has the authority to adopt rules governing
7

personnel matters pursuant to sections 1001.42(5), 1012.22(1), and 1012.23,
Florida Statutes.
22. The School Board has the burden to establish, by a preponderance of
the evidence the grounds for disciplining Respondent. See, e.g., McNeill v.
Pinellas Cnty. Sch. Bd., 678 So. 2d 476, 477 (Fla. 2d DCA 1996); Sublett v.
Sumter Cnty. Sch. Bd., 664 So. 2d 1178, 1179 (Fla. 5th DCA 1995); Allen v.
Sch. Bd. of Dade Cnty., 571 So. 2d 568, 569 (Fla. 3d DCA 1990); Dileo v. Sch.
Bd. of Dade Cnty., 569 So. 2d 883, 884 (Fla. 3d DCA 1990).
23. The preponderance of the evidence standard requires proof by “the
greater weight of the evidence” or evidence that “more likely than not” tends
to prove a certain proposition. See Gross v. Lyons, 763 So. 2d 276, 280 n.l
(Fla. 2000); see also Williams v. Eau Claire Pub. Sch., 397 F.3d 441, 446 (6th
Cir. 2005)(holding trial court properly defined the preponderance of the
evidence standard as “such evidence as, when considered and compared with
that opposed to it, has more convincing force and produces ... [a] belief that
what is sought to be proved is more likely true than not true”).
24. In Florida, the district superintendent has the authority to make
recommendations for dismissal of school board employees. The school board
has the authority to terminate or suspend without pay school board
instructional staff with professional service contracts for “just cause.”
§§ 1001.42(5), 1012.22(l)(f), and 1012.33(6)(a), Fla. Stat.
25. School Board Policy 3121 provides Conditions for Employment and Re-
employment of Instructional Staff as follows:
Applicants for employment or re-employment must
submit an employment application, a copy of the
social security card with correct name, and a
minimum of three (3) acceptable references.
Candidates shall meet the School Board’s hiring
guidelines and employment prerequisites prior to
consideration for any vacancy.
Failure of candidates to adhere to the time schedule
established for submission of documents may be
cause for failure to employ or for dismissal.
8

False or misleading statements or answers or
omissions made by a person in connection with
seeking employment may bar a person from
employment with the Board or, if discovered after
employment, may result in disciplinary action,
including termination upon the recommendation of
the Superintendent and the approval of the Board.
Each case shall be considered on its own merits.
26. School Board Policy 3140 provides, for the Suspension or Dismissal of
Instructional Staff, in pertinent part, as follows:
It is the desire of the School Board to maintain a
staff of well-trained, competent instructional
employees in order to offer comprehensive services
to the students of this District.
Upon the recommendation of the Superintendent,
an employee may be suspended from duty by the
Board. The Superintendent, however, shall have the
authority to suspend members of the instructional
staff and other school employees during emergencies
for a period extending to and including the day of the
next regular or special meeting of the Board and
notify the Board immediately of such suspension.
Any instructional personnel may be suspended or
dismissed at any time during the term of the
contract for just cause as defined below. The Board
must notify the employee whenever charges are
made and may suspend such person without pay. As
defined by State law, “just cause” includes, but is not
limited to:
A. immorality;
B. misconduct in office;
C. incompetency;
D. gross insubordination;
E. willful neglect of duty;
9

F. being convicted or found guilty of, or entering a
plea of guilty regardless of adjudication of guilt, any
crime involving moral turpitude.
* * *
Any member of the instructional staff who is
employed under an annual contract may be
suspended or dismissed at any time during the term
of his/her contract for cause pursuant to provisions
of Florida statutes.
Any member of the instructional staff who is under
continuing contract may be suspended or dismissed
at any time during the school year pursuant to the
provisions set forth in State law.
Policy 8141 sets forth the procedures for mandatory
reporting of alleged misconduct by instructional
staff members to the Florida Department of
Education. Additionally, parental notification of
certain misconduct is required in accordance with
Policy 8141.
The Superintendent shall determine the nature and
effective date of the suspension or dismissal.
27. School Board Policy 3210 provides, for the Standard of Ethical
Conduct, in pertinent part, as follows:
Instructional staff members shall be guided by and
adhere to the following ethical principles:
A. The instructional staff member values the worth
and dignity of every person, the pursuit of truth,
devotion to excellence, acquisition of knowledge, and
the nurture of democratic citizenship. Essential to
the achievement of these standards are the freedom
to learn and to teach and the guarantee of equal
opportunity for all.
B. The instructional staff member’s primary
professional concern will always be for the student
and for the development of the student’s potential.
The instructional staff member will, therefore, strive
10

for professional growth and will seek to exercise the
best professional judgment and integrity.
C. The instructional staff member strives to achieve
and sustain the highest degree of ethical conduct
because s/he is aware of the importance of
maintaining the respect and confidence of one’s
colleagues, of students, of parents, and of other
members of the community.
District instructional staff members shall comply
with the following disciplinary principles. Violation
of any of these principles shall subject the individual
to revocation or suspension of the individual
instructional staff member’s certificate, or the other
penalties as provided by law.
* * *
C. Obligation to the profession of education requires
that the District instructional staff member shall:
* * *
13. self-report within forty-eight (48) hours to a
District authority, as determined by the
Superintendent, any arrest for a felony or
misdemeanor offense listed in F.S. 435.04, including
any arrests/charges involving the abuse of a child or
the sale and/or possession of a controlled substance.
Such self-report is not to be considered an admission
of guilt nor shall such self-report be admissible for
any purpose in any proceeding, civil or criminal,
administrative or judicial, investigatory or
adjudicatory. In addition, District instructional staff
members shall self-report any conviction, finding of
guilt, withholding of adjudication, commitment to a
pretrial diversion program, or entering of a plea of
guilty or Nolo Contendere for any criminal offense
other than a minor traffic violation within forty-
eight (48) hours after the final judgment. When
handling sealed and expunged records disclosed
under this rule, school districts shall comply with
11

the confidentiality provisions of F.S. 943.0585(4)(c)
and 943.059(4)(c)
28. School Board Policy 3231 for Outside Activities of Staff in pertinent,
part provides:
Instructional staff members should avoid situations
in which their personal interests, activities, and
associations conflict with the interests of the
District. If such situations threaten a staff member's
effectiveness within the school system, the
Superintendent and/or School Board shall evaluate
the impact of such interest, activity, or association
upon the instructional staff member's
responsibilities.
29. Florida Administrative Code Rule 6A-5.056 defines “just cause” as the
basis for dismissal actions against instructional personnel:
6A-5.056 Criteria for Suspension and Dismissal.
“Just cause” means cause that is legally sufficient.
Each of the charges upon which just cause for a
dismissal action against specified school personnel
may be pursued are set forth in sections 1012.33 and
1012.335, F.S. In fulfillment of these laws, the basis
for each such charge is hereby defined:
(2) “Misconduct in Office” means one or more of the
following:
(a) A violation of the Code of Ethics of the Education
Profession in Florida as adopted in Rule 6B-1.001,
F.A.C.;
(b) A violation of the Principles of Professional
Conduct for the Education Profession in Florida as
adopted in Rule 6B-1.006, F.A.C.;
(c) violation of the adopted school board rules;
(d) Behavior that disrupts the student’s learning
environment; or
12

(e) Behavior that reduces the teacher’s ability or his
or her colleagues’ ability to effectively perform
duties.
30. CBA Section 4.4, Just Cause (found beginning on CBA page 5),
provides, in relevant part:
No teacher will be disciplined, reprimanded,
suspended, terminated or otherwise deprived of
fringe benefits or contractual rights during the term
of his/her contract without just cause ... . Any
teacher terminated during the term of his/her
contract shall be entitled to a fair hearing based on
due process.
31. CBA Section 4.4-1, the Progressive Discipline Policy (found beginning
on CBA page 5), provides, in relevant part:
Progressive discipline shall be followed, except in
cases where the course of conduct or the severity of
the offense justifies otherwise. Unusual
circumstances may justify suspension with pay.
Progressive discipline shall be administered in the
following steps:
(1) verbal warning in a conference with the teacher.
(A written confirmation of a verbal warning is not a
written reprimand);
(2) dated written reprimand following a conference;
(3) suspension without pay for up to five days by the
Superintendent; and
(4) termination
32. Mr. Griffin meets the definition of “instructional personnel” set forth
in section 1012.01(2). Mr. Griffin is a long-time teacher for the School Board
whose employment can be terminated only for “just cause.” The School Board
has the authority to suspend or terminate instructional staff pursuant to
sections 1012.22(1)(f) and 1012.33(6)(a).
13

33. Section 435.04 provides, in pertinent part:
(2) The security background investigations under
this section must ensure that persons subject to this
section have not been arrested for and are awaiting
final disposition of; have not been found guilty of,
regardless of adjudication, or entered a plea of nolo
contendere or guilty to; or have not been adjudicated
delinquent and the record has not been sealed or
expunged for, any offense prohibited under any of
the following provisions of state law or similar law
of another jurisdiction:
* * *
(k) Chapter 784, relating to assault, battery, and
culpable negligence, if the offense was a felony.
* * *
(r) § 787.02, relating to false imprisonment.
* * *
(hh) § 810.02, relating to burglary.
34. Superintendent Heid initiated this action in mid-December 2024,
alleging Respondent violated School Board Policy 3210–Standards of Ethical
Conduct. On January 10, 2025, Respondent was notified that he was
suspended with pay, and Superintendent Heid was recommending the School
Board terminate Respondent’s employment at the next School Board
meeting. Two weeks later, Mr. Griffin was suspended without pay.
35. Mr. Griffin’s request for hearing afforded him the administrative
hearing as provided in the CBA.
36. Whether Respondent committed the alleged violations is a question of
ultimate fact to be determined by the trier of fact (the ALJ) in the context of
each alleged violation. Holmes v. Turlington, 480 So. 2d 150, 153 (Fla. 1985);
14

McKinney v. Castor, 667 So. 2d 387, 389 (Fla. 1st DCA 1995); Langston v.
Jamerson, 653 So. 2d 489, 491 (Fla. 1st DCA 1995).
Summary
37. Respondent argues that his arrest for three felonies, which were
resolved through a plea agreement to two misdemeanors, does not establish
that his behavior “disrupted any student’s learning environment or reduced
his ability” to effectively perform his duties. Even if it is established that
Mr. Griffin, a long-time employee of the School Board who has received
“effective or highly effective” evaluations, there is no rationalization sufficient
to discount the actions he took in mid-December 2024, that led to his felony
arrest.
38. Respondent’s actions could not help but effect the way he is viewed by
his peers, the parents, or students for that matter. His judgment is
questionable. Although he was ordered to attend an anger management class,
no testimony was ever elicited as to his completion of that class or what
actions he has taken to control what appears to be his aggressive behavior.
39. Respondent has several blemishes including discipline by the School
Board and FDOE on his record and it appears he wants to continue teaching
without suffering consequences for those December 2024 actions. There is no
question that Mr. Griffin failed to exercise his best judgment when he
battered3 another person.
40. In sum, based on the testimony and evidence produced during the
hearing, the School Board proved, by a preponderance of the evidence, that
Respondent’s actions warrant discipline. The School Board established legally
sufficient grounds to terminate Respondent’s employment.
3 Call it Felony Battery or Simple Battery – it was battery. “Any unlawful beating, or other
wrongful physical violence or constraint inflicted on a human being without his consent.” See
Black’s Law Dictionary (12LL Edition 2024).
15

RECOMMENDATION
Based on the foregoing Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, it is
RECOMMENDED that Petitioner, Polk County School Board, enter a final
order terminating the employment of Respondent, Thomas Griffin.
DONE AND ENTERED this 25th day of March, 2026, in Tallahassee,
Leon County, Florida.

STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES
Whether just cause exists for Petitioner, the Polk County School Board
(the School Board), to discipline Respondent, Thomas B. Griffin, and, if so,
whether termination of Respondent’s employment is the appropriate

discipline. ,

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT

On December 19, 2025, Brian Warren, the Associate Superintendent Chief
of Labor and Employee Relations, issued a letter to Respondent. This letter
reminded Mr. Griffin that he remained on “unpaid Suspension, continuing
[his] status from January 29, 2025, ... based on alleged violations of Polk
County School Board Policies, including but not limited to, 3121.01-
Background Screening and Employment History Checks and 3210 —
Standards of Ethical Conduct.” This letter also provided that Superintendent
Frederick R. Heid would recommend to the School Board that Mr. Griffin’s
employment with the School Board be terminated effective January 28, 2026.

On December 23, 2025, Respondent, through his attorney, timely
requested a formal appeal hearing challenging the proposed termination of
his employment. On January 8, 2026, the School Board submitted a request

to DOAH for assignment of an ALJ to “hear a teacher termination case.”

Following receipt of a Joint Response to Initial Order, the Zoom hearing
was scheduled for February 27, 2026, and completed on that date. The
parties filed a Joint Pre-Hearing Stipulation that identified limited facts for
which the parties agreed no evidence would be required at hearing. Those
facts are incorporated into the Findings of Fact to the extent relevant and

FINDINGS OF FACT

Based on the credibility of the witnesses who testified, the documentary

Witnesses and Duties

2. *Respondent is a teacher employed by the School Board, working under
the School Board and the Polk Education Association, Inc.’s, Teacher
Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA). Mr. Griffin worked with students
with disabilities as a full-time math teacher.

3. Brian Warren is currently employed by the School Board as the chief of
labor and employee relations. Mr. Warren oversees all of the School Board’s
contract negotiations and disciplines. Mr. Warren was the Associate
Superintendent or Chief of the School Board’s Human Resource Services

4, Laura McCabe is the Director of Labor and Employee Relations in HRS
for the School Board. Ms. McCabe is responsible for mainly Level 2

medical leaves of absence, collective bargaining matters, negotiations, and

team.

Issue of the Case

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
‘20. DOAH has jurisdiction over the subject matter and parties to this
proceeding pursuant to sections 120.569, 120.57(1), and 1012.33(6)(a)2.
21. The School Board is the duly-constituted governing body of the School
District of Polk County. Art. IX, § 4, Fla. Const.; §§ 1001.30 and 1001.33, Fla.
Stat. A district school board has the authority to adopt rules governing

personnel matters pursuant to sections 1001.42(5), 1012.22(1), and 1012.23,
Florida Statutes.

22. The School Board has the burden to establish, by a preponderance of
the evidence the grounds for disciplining Respondent. See, e.g., McNeill v.
Pinellas Cnty. Sch. Bd., 678 So. 2d 476, 477 (Fla. 2d DCA 1996); Sublet v.
Sumter Cnty. Sch. Bd., 664 So. 2d 1178, 1179 (Fla. 5th DCA 1995); Allen v.
Sch, Bd. of Dade Cnty., 571 So. 2d 568, 569 (Fla. 3d DCA 1990); Dileo v. Sch.
Bd. of Dade Cnity., 569 So. 2d 883, 884 (Fla. 3d DCA 1990). |

23. The preponderance of the evidence standard requires proof by “the
greater weight of the evidence” or evidence that “more likely than not” tends
to prove a certain proposition. See Gross v. Lyons, 763 So. 2d 276, 280 nl
(Fla. 2000); see also Williams v. Eau Claire Pub. Sch., 397 F.3d 441, 446 (6th
Cir. 2005)(holding trial court properly defined the preponderance of the
evidence standard as “such evidence as, when considered and compared with
that opposed to it, has more convincing force and produces ... [a] belief that
what is sought to be proved is more likely true than not true”).

24. In Florida, the district superintendent has the authority to make
recommendations for dismissal of school board employees. The school board
has the authority to terminate or suspend without pay school board
instructional staff with professional service contracts for “just cause.”

§§ 1001.42(5), 1012.22), and 1012.33(6)(a), Fla. Stat.

alleging Respondent violated School Board Policy 3210-Standards of Ethical
Conduct. On January 10, 2025, Respondent was notified that he was
suspended with pay, and Superintendent Heid was recommending the School
Board terminate Respondent’s employment at the next School Board

35. Mr. Griffin’s request for hearing afforded him the administrative

36. Whether Respondent committed the alleged violations is a question of

each alleged violation. Holmes v. Turlington, 480 So. 2d 150, 153 (Fla. 1985);

14

McKinney v. Castor, 667 So. 2d 387, 389 (Fla. 1st DCA 1995); Langston v.

37. Respondent argues that his arrest for three felonies, which were
resolved through a plea agreement to two misdemeanors, does not establish
that his behavior “disrupted any student’s learning environment or reduced
his ability” to effectively perform his duties. Even if it is established that
Mr. Griffin, a long-time employee of the School Board who has received
“effective or highly effective” evaluations, there is no rationalization sufficient
to discount the actions he took in mid-December 2024, that led to his felony
arrest.

38. Respondent’s actions could not help but effect the way he is viewed by
his peers, the parents, or students for that matter. His judgment is
questionable. Although he was ordered to attend an anger management class,
no testimony was ever elicited as to his completion of that class or what
actions he has taken to control what appears to be his aggressive behavior.

39. Respondent has several blemishes including discipline by the School
Board and FDOE on his record and it appears he wants to continue teaching
without suffering consequences for those December 2024 actions. There is no
question that Mr. Griffin failed to exercise his best judgment when he
battered’ another person.

40. In sum, based on the testimony and evidence produced during the
hearing, the School Board proved, by a preponderance of the evidence, that
Respondent’s actions warrant discipline. The School Board established legally

sufficient grounds to terminate Respondent’s employment.

STATEMENT OF THE ISSUE
Whether Petitioner proved that Respondent engaged in unlawful
retaliation against Petitioner at his place of employment, in violation of
section 760.10, Florida Statutes (2023), as alleged.1
1 The 2022 version of chapter 760, which was in effect at the time of the most recent alleged
discriminatory conduct, applies to this proceeding.

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
On June 3, 2025, Petitioner, Luther Saunders ("Petitioner" or "Saunders"),
filed an Employment Complaint of Discrimination with the Florida
Commission on Human Relations ("FCHR") alleging that Respondent,
Miami-Dade County ("Respondent" or the "County"), Department of Transit
and Public Works ("DTPW") had engaged in unlawful retaliation against him.
Following an investigation of the alleged discriminatory conduct, on
November 25, 2025, FCHR issued a Determination: No Reasonable Cause,
concluding that it was unlikely that unlawful discrimination occurred.
Pursuant to the Notice of Determination: No Reasonable Cause, Saunders
filed a Petition for Relief on December 28, 2025, reiterating his allegations of
unlawful work retaliation and requesting an administrative hearing
pursuant to sections 120.569 and 120.57(1), Florida Statutes.
This matter was referred to DOAH for assignment to an administrative
law judge to conduct a final hearing on the complaint of discrimination, and
his subsequent petition. The final hearing was conducted over two days, on
April 13 and 22, 2026.
Saunders testified on his own behalf and presented the testimony from
current or former DTPW employees, Ronessa Wilson, Manny Fresnedo, and
James Graham. Both parties presented the testimony of Lead Transit
Operations Supervisor ("TOS") Carlos Robledo.
The County presented testimony of then–Acting Section Chief Elena
Najarro; Lead TOSs Lakeisha Terrell, Rene Molina, Cedric Dallas; TOS and
Union Representative Ernest Charles; TOS Andrew Allen; Superintendent
Omar Yoda; General Superintendent Schneider St. Preux; DTPW Office of
2

Civil Rights and Labor Relations Manager Cindy LaBranche; and Deputy
Director Sean Adgerson. Petitioner's Composite Exhibits A, B, C, and D were
admitted into evidence. Respondent's Exhibits 1, 2, and 3 were also admitted
into evidence.
The three-volume Transcript of the final hearing was filed on May 15,
2026. Proposed recommended orders for both parties were filed, reviewed,
and considered before preparing this Recommended Order.
References to statutes, rules, or policies refer to those in effect on the date
of the action, omission, or occurrence. Exhibits are referred to as "Pet. Ex."

FINDINGS OF FACT
The undersigned makes the following findings of material and relevant
facts:
Saunders's Work Background
1. Saunders worked as a bus operator for the County beginning December
2014, and served as an out-of-class instructor for new bus operator trainees,
from August 2022 to November 2023.
2. In November 2023, Saunders was promoted to TOS and served a
12-month probationary period under Superintendent Omar Yoda.
3. Following his promotion, Saunders completed an initial training
program of approximately four months under the instruction of Lead TOSs
Rene Molina and Cedric Dallas, among others.
The TOS Position and Probationary Process
4. Under the County Personnel Rules for the Classified Service,
Chapter III, Section 11, the probationary period is an integral and necessary
part of the examination process for promoted employees. Probation is
3

designed to closely observe an employee's work and provides the option to fail
an employee whose performance does not meet the required standards.
5. Significantly, a department head or authorized designee may remove or
demote a probationary employee at any time prior to the expiration of the
probationary period, without charges and without the right of appeal.
6. A probationary TOS employee who fails probation is demoted and
returns to the position he/she held prior to promotion. Resp. Ex. 1, at 4 and 5.
7. A TOS performs two broad categories of duties. First, a TOS working an
indoor assignment operates from a dispatch window at a bus garage, where
the TOS may assign work to bus operators, manages bus availability, assigns
buses to departing operators, handles schedule adjustments in real time, and
tracks on-time performance. This role requires multitasking simultaneous
and pressing demands within short timeframes.
8. Second, a TOS works road assignment patrol zones in a County car,
where he/she may respond to accidents and incidents, communicates with
central control, and manages terminals.
9. The process for failing a probationary TOS employee at DTPW requires
the superintendent to prepare a memorandum documenting performance
concerns and attaching supporting documentation, followed by concurrences
from several supervisory/management personnel, including the section chief,
general superintendent, assistant director, as well as a review by the Office of
Civil Rights and Labor Relations. Ultimately, the deputy director makes the
final decision.

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
78. DOAH has jurisdiction over the parties and subject matter of this
proceeding pursuant to sections 120.569, 120.57(1), and 760.11.
79. The Petitioner's case is based upon a violation of section 760.10(7)
prohibiting retaliation.
80. The Florida Civil Rights Act of 1992 ("FCRA") prohibits retaliation
against any person because that person has opposed a practice which is an
unlawful employment practice:
It is an unlawful employment practice for an
employer … to discriminate against any person
because that person has opposed any practice which
is an unlawful employment practice under this
section, or because that person has made a charge,
testified, assisted, or participated in any manner in
an investigation, proceeding, or hearing under this
section.
§ 760.10(7), Fla. Stat.
14

81. The FCRA is modeled after Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1965
("Title VII"), the federal antidiscrimination law. As a result, case law
interpreting Title VII is applicable to proceedings under the FCRA. Palm
Beach Cty. Sch. Bd. v. Wright, 217 So. 3d 163, 165 (Fla. 4th DCA 2017)
(en banc).
82. To arrive at the proper disposition of this case, the undersigned must
consider the elements of a retaliation claim under chapter 760.
83. Under the law, to establish a claim of retaliation, Saunders
must prove three things: (1) that he "engaged in a statutorily protected
activity," (2) that he "suffered an adverse action," and (3) that "the adverse
action was causally related to the protected activity." Gogel v. Kia Motors
Mfg. of Ga., Inc., 967 F.3d 1121, 1134 (11th Cir. 2020) (en banc).
84. The burden of proof is on Saunders to establish each element by a
preponderance of the evidence, and that unlawful retaliation occurred.
McAlpin v. Sneads, 61 F.4th 916, 927 (11th Cir. 2023).
85. Florida courts follow the same analysis for a retaliation claim.
See Buade v. Terra Grp., LLC, 259 So. 3d 219, 222 (Fla. 3d DCA 2018);
Carter v. Health Mgmt. Assocs., 989 So. 2d 1258, 1263 (Fla. 2d DCA 2008).2
86. Recently, in Kiernan v. ReviveMD305, 412 So. 3d 156 (Fla. 3rd DCA
2025), the Florida Third District Court of Appeals elaborated on additional
considerations in a retaliation case, and added:
"Opposing sexual harassment by reporting it to an
employer may qualify as statutorily protected
activity, see Vill. of Tequesta v. Luscavich, 240 So.
3d 733 (Fla. 4th DCA 2018), but a plaintiff-employee
must show that she "had a good faith, reasonable
belief that the employer was engaged in unlawful
employment practices." Hunsaker v. Found.
Partners Grp., LLC, No. 6:18-cv-1996-Orl-22DCI,
2020 WL 10355118 at *10 (M.D. Fla. 2020). "The
opposition must be directed at an unlawful
employment practice of an employer, not an act of
2 The parties agree that these are the elements to prove a claim of retaliation by Saunders.
15

discrimination by a private individual." Little v.
United Techs., 103 F. 3d 956, 959 (11th Cir. 1997)
(citation omitted).
In addition, the "plaintiff must show both that: (1)
she subjectively believed her employer engaged in
an unlawful practice, and (2) that this belief 'was
objectively reasonable in light of the facts and record
presented.'" Small v. City of Hollywood, 661
F.Supp.3d 1187, 1202-03 (S.D. Fla. 2023) (noting
"complaints about single instances of 'uncalled for,
ugly, racists statements' are not the kind of activity
protected by Title VII." (citation omitted)) (emphasis
added).
87. With this legal background in mind, and as more fully explained
below, the undersigned concludes that Saunders marginally proved the first
element ("he engaged in a statutorily protected activity"), satisfied the second
element ("he suffered an adverse action"), but Saunders failed in his proof
regarding the third element ("the adverse action was causally related to the
protected activity").
88. Whether Saunders had an honest or good faith belief that the County
discriminated against him or other employees is a factual question and, like
all matters of credibility, is solely for the factfinder to assess and determine.
See United States v. Grushko, 50 F.4th 1, 11 (11th Cir. 2022). The factfinder
may credit all, some, or none of a witness's testimony. AM Grand Court
Lakes, LLC v. Rockhill Ins. Co., 68 F.4th 1354, 1363-64 (11th Cir. 2023).
89. "The objective reasonableness of an employee's belief that [his]
employer has engaged in an unlawful employment practice must be
measured against existing substantive law." Clover v. Total Sys. Servs., Inc.,
176 F.3d 1346, 1351 (11th Cir. 1999). In this instance, Saunders would have
an objectively reasonable belief if a reasonable person would, under the
circumstances, believe that the County retaliated against him because of his
complaints or opposition to racial discrimination in his workplace.
16

First Element–Saunders Proved that He Engaged in Protected Activity
90. In this case, Saunders asserted two primary forms of protected
activity: (1) statements he made during a phone call with Yoda on April 18,
2024, about Yoda's alleged history of treating black employees poorly; and
(2) a skin-rubbing gesture during a subsequent meeting.
91. In a phone call with Yoda, Saunders claims that he complained, or
raised the point, that Yoda had a history of treating black employees poorly.
The undersigned credits this testimony by Saunders.
92. This, of course, was only an accusation, but it was premised on
Saunders's observations and his opinion of his treatment in the workplace
over time. It also took into account his knowledge regarding the history of
other black employees' reporting complaints of racial discrimination to FCHR
(Graham and Ferguson).
93. While these other complaints may have gone "unfounded," they
provided, at least, a basis for Saunders to believe that racial discrimination
was going on in his workplace. That, together with his own perceived
treatment, gave him a reasonable belief that discrimination existed.
94. The undersigned stresses that there is no independent finding being
made that racial discrimination was taking place–only that Saunders had a
subjective and reasonably objective belief that this environment existed.
95. The second allegation of protected activity is when Saunders rubbed
his forearm and said "I know what this is about" during the in-person
meeting with Yoda, Terrell, and the Union Representative Charles.
96. All three acknowledged during the hearing that they saw Saunders
make the gesture. Yoda and Terrell also testified that they knew, by the
gesture, that Saunders was pointing out he felt there was racial hostility in
the workplace.
17

97. The question is whether, in context, this gesture communicated a
good faith, objectively reasonable belief by Saunders that the County was
engaged in an unlawful employment practice. The undersigned finds that it
did.
98. The gesture occurred during a heated confrontation with Yoda, while
Yoda was attempting to address performance issues.
99. Both Yoda and Terrell reasonably understood this gesture was
Saunders's way of communicating or expressing to Yoda that he felt that
racial discrimination existed in the workplace. The point was clearly made by
Saunders. It may have been a crude way of doing so, but sometimes actions
do speak louder than words.
100. Nonetheless, it was his way of expressing his opposition to the
practice and culture that he believed existed at DTPW. Opposition to
unlawful practices can occur in a variety of ways and forms. Kiernan, 412
So. 3d at 156.
Second Element–Saunders Proved That Failure of Probation is an Adverse
Employment Action
101. The parties do not dispute that the failure of probation and return to
the bus operator position constitutes an adverse employment action within
the meaning of section 760.10(7). As a result, this second listed element for a
claim of retaliation under section 760.10 (7) was established.
Third Element–Saunders Failed to Prove a Casual Connection Between His
Protected Activity and the Above Employment Action
102. At this juncture in the case analysis, Saunders proof and case take a
fatal turn. Saunders failure to prove this final element involved a broad
range of evidentiary points and topics that scuttle or totally undermine
Saunders proof that a causal connection existed.
18

103. To start, direct evidence of the unreasonableness of Saunders's
argument that the County retaliated against him for his opposition, is found
in the comparator record of how other African Americans were treated
regarding TOS promotions.
104. For example, three black TOS trainees–Allen, Roberts, and Woods–
passed probation under the same superintendent during the same time
frame. Allen, who was in the same training class, testified that Yoda was a
stand-up manager and that race never affected their interactions.
105. Lead TOS Robledo, who worked alongside all four probationary
employees, confirmed that all three had some dispatch difficulties and still
passed, but Saunders "probably had the most errors."
106. Saunders cannot convincingly demonstrate retaliation where three
black colleagues in the same classification succeeded under the same
supervisor during the same time period, particularly where the independent
Office of Civil Rights and Labor Relations investigation found no evidence for
his retaliation claims. Further, his own union representative–who was
present at the April 18, 2024, meeting–did not witness racial animus by Yoda
nor did he file a grievance on Saunders's behalf.
107. Most significantly, the record is replete with numerous examples of
poor and deficient work performance by Saunders during his probationary
period. His refusal to accept more training, refusal to adapt and embrace the
multitasking required by the TOS job, and the insubordinate way he acted on
phone calls and in meetings with Yoda, were glaring. All provided a sound,
legitimate, and non-discriminatory basis to fail his probation.
108. At bottom, "Title VII's anti-retaliation provisions do not allow
employees who are already on thin ice to insulate themselves against
termination or discipline by preemptively making a discrimination
complaint." Alvarez v. Royal Atl. Devs., Inc., 610 F.3d 1253, 1270 (11th Cir.
2010).
19

109. Other evidence supports a conclusion that Saunders failed to
establish the third element–a causal connection between his protected
activity and the adverse employment action.
110. To establish a causal connection that an employee suffered an
adverse employment action "because of" his protected activity, courts usually
"look only to the conduct of the decisionmaker–the party with the 'power to
actually [affect] the employee's [status].'" Lewis v. City of Union City, 934
F.3d 1169, 1196 (11th Cir. 2019) (en banc) (Tjoflat, J., concurring in part and
dissenting in part) (quoting Stimpson v. City of Tuscaloosa, 186 F.3d 1328,
1331 (11th Cir. 1999)).
111. In Saunders's case, the final decisionmaker was Deputy Director
Adgerson. He testified unequivocally that he had no knowledge of any
protected activity–the phone call with Yoda or the skin-rubbing gesture–at
the time he made his decision to fail Saunders's probation.
112. In addition, Adgerson had no direct communication with Yoda about
Saunders at any point during or after the failure-of-probation process.
113. Adgerson was not motivated to retaliate since he had no
knowledge of the two instances of Saunders's opposition.
114. While the cat's paw theory was not advanced by Petitioner in his
proposed recommended order, it is briefly addressed and dismissed as
inapplicable to this case. The cat's paw theory derives from a fable conceived
by Aesop and injected into United States employment discrimination law by
Judge Posner in 1990. See Staub v. Proctor Hosp., 562 U.S. 411, 422 n.1
(2011).
115. Under the cat's paw theory, the animus of a biased supervisor who
reports to the decisionmaker can be imputed to the decisionmaker. Petitioner
must prove that: (1) the reporting supervisor acted with retaliatory animus;
(2) the supervisor intended to cause an adverse employment action; and
(3) the supervisor's biased act was the but-for cause of the ultimate adverse
action. See Staub, 562 U.S. at 422.
20

116. In general terms, the cat's paw theory seeks to hold an employer
liable for the animus of a supervisor who was not charged with making the
ultimate adverse employment decision, but improperly influenced the final
decision maker. Brnovich v. Democratic Nat'l Comm., 594 U.S. 647, 689
(2021).
117. However, the theory is not available in retaliation cases under Title
VII or the FCRA.
118. "Title VII retaliation claims require proof that the desire to retaliate
was the but-for cause of the challenged employment action." Univ. of Tex. Sw.
Med. Ctr. v. Nassar, 570 U.S. 338, 352 (2013). "In other words, a plaintiff
must prove that had [he] not engaged in the protected conduct," he would not
have suffered the adverse employment action. Gogel, 967 F.3d at 1135 (11th
Cir. 2020) (en banc).
119. More to the point, "[a] 'but-for' cause requires a closer link than mere
proximate causation; it requires that the proscribed animus have a
determinative influence on the employer's adverse decision." Sims v. MVM,
Inc., 704 F.3d 1327, 1335–36 (11th Cir. 2013).
120. Because Title VII retaliation claims require a "but-for" link between
the retaliatory animus and the adverse employment action, as opposed to
showing that the animus was merely a motivating factor in the decision, the
cat's paw theory "does not fit" Title VII retaliation claims. Mosley v. Preston
Cycles W., LLC, No. 21-13527, 2024 WL 2873720, at *5–6 (11th Cir. June 7,
2024) (citing Sims, 704 F.3d at 1336); see also Duncan v. Ala., 734 F. App'x
637, 640 (11th Cir. 2018) (cat's paw "is inappropriate when the statute
requires but-for causation").
121. The same limitation is true in Florida under chapter 760.10(7). See
Palm Beach Cnty. Sch. Bd. v. Wright, 217 So. 3d 163 (Fla. 4th DCA 2017) (en
banc) (The cat's paw theory does not apply to a FCRA retaliation case since it
applies a "but-for" causation standard.).
21

122. Ultimately, the undersigned was convinced that Saunders's failure of
probation as a TOS was not caused by or related to his opposition to Yoda
about his treatment of other black employees.
123. Rather, he failed probation because Yoda and other management
personnel reasonably concluded that his work performance, attitude, and
capabilities were not up to the standards expected for a TOS at DTPW.
124. In sum, the undersigned finds that Saunders has failed to prove by
a preponderance of the evidence that his protected activity was the but-for
cause of the failure of his probation. He has introduced no evidence from
which the undersigned could conclude that, absent the protected activity, the
failure of probation would not have occurred.
125. Based on the foregoing, the undersigned concludes that Petitioner
has failed to carry his burden to establish that Respondent, through its
employees, engaged in conduct that constituted retaliation against Petitioner,
in violation of section 760.10(7).
RECOMMENDATION
Based on the foregoing Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, it is
RECOMMENDED that the Florida Commission on Human Relations issue
a final order dismissing the Petition for Relief finding that Miami-Dade
County did not commit an unlawful employment practice in violation of
section 760.10(7).

was assigned to the undersigned and an arbitration hearing was scheduled
for 9:00 a.m., on March 25, 2026, via Zoom.1
Petitioners did not appear at the arbitration hearing. Citizens was
present. The arbitrator waited until 9:15 a.m., and, with no appearance by
Petitioners or their counsel, the arbitrator adjourned the hearing.
1 This is an arbitration, not a chapter 120 administrative proceeding or a civil action. By the
parties' agreement and the operation of law, this arbitration is mandatory, binding, and

96, 98 (Fla. 4th DCA 2021); Mejia v. Citizens Prop. Ins. Corp., 161 So. 3d 576,
578 (Fla. 2d DCA 2014). Accordingly, Petitioners' loss is not covered by the
Citizens policy and the amount of policy benefits payable on this insurance
claim is zero dollars.
